Understanding Issues, Causes and Solutions in Open-Source LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

Asad Ur Rehman asadurrehman@whu.edu.cn    Syed Mohammad Kashif smkashif145@gmail.com    Ruiyin Li ryli_cs@whu.edu.cn    Peng Liang liangp@whu.edu.cn Address: School of Computer Science, Wuhan University, China    Zengyang Li zengyangli@ccnu.edu.cn Address: School of Computer Science & Hubei Provincial Key Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence and Smart Learning, Central China Normal University, China    Arif Ali Khan arif.khan@oulu.fi Address: M3S Empirical Software Engineering Research Unit, University of Oulu, Finland
Abstract

With the advancement of LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS), an increasing number of open-source projects are adopting multi-agent architectures as the foundation of their core functionality. Although research and practice on MAS have attracted considerable attention, limited studies have explored the challenges faced by practitioners of open-source LLM-based MAS, the causes of these challenges, and potential solutions. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study to understand the issues that practitioners encounter when developing and using open-source LLM-based MAS, the possible causes of these issues, and potential solutions. We collected 22,848 closed issues from 21 open-source LLM-based MAS and applied a mixed automated and manual filtering approach to reduce the dataset to 944 issues related to LLM-based MAS. We then analyzed these issues to understand the frequent issues encountered by practitioners, their underlying causes, and potential solutions. Our study results show that (1) Orchestration & Execution Issue is the most common issue faced by practitioners, (2) Workflow Problem, Tool Integration Problem, and Memory Problem are identified as the most frequent causes of the issues, and (3) Optimize Workflow is the predominant solution to the issues. Based on the study results, we derive empirically grounded implications for practitioners and researchers aimed at improving orchestration, tool integration, and memory mechanisms in LLM-based MAS.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming the landscape of software development, moving us beyond simple coding copilots to a future where specialized LLM-powered agents actively collaborate like a digital team (Hou et al., 2024). Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022 (OpenAI, 2025a), research on LLMs has grown rapidly (Zhao et al., 2023a). The software engineering (SE) community quickly recognized their potential and began applying LLMs throughout the software development lifecycle (Hou et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024). Early studies examined single-agent scenarios, where an LLM assists developers with code generation, code review, software testing, and requirements documentation (Fan et al., 2023).

Recent advances in multi-agent frameworks have enabled the development of LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS), in which multiple specialized LLM-powered agents communicate, coordinate, and collaborate to accomplish complex, sequential software engineering tasks that were previously too difficult for a single LLM agent (He et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2026). This architectural approach is well-suited for complex end-to-end software processes because it addresses the inherent limitations of individual LLMs, including limited context windows, error propagation, and difficulties in managing complex software development workflows (He et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024).

Meanwhile, software practitioners are increasingly integrating LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) into their software projects. Frameworks such as LangChain and Semantic Kernel facilitate the development of these systems, supporting a wide range of applications from code generation to system design (Chase, 2024; Microsoft, 2024). Recent surveys have examined the use of LLMs in SE, analyzing model usage, dataset creation, and evaluation methods (Hou et al., 2024). Despite the rapid adoption and significant potential of LLM-based MAS (Guo et al., 2024), there remains a lack of empirical studies regarding the challenges associated with their development and maintenance in real-world contexts. From an SE perspective, the complexity of agent coordination, planning, and interaction introduces novel challenges that are not yet fully understood.

This study addresses this gap by conducting a comprehensive empirical analysis of prominent open-source systems (OSS) that incorporate LLM-based MAS as core architectural components. We collected 22,848 closed issues from relevant GitHub repositories whose documentation explicitly describes them as MAS projects. GitHub is the leading platform for hosting OSS projects and is widely used in empirical SE research (Alrashedy and Binjahlan, 2024). Our approach of analyzing closed issues from prominent OSS projects follows well-established practices in empirical SE (Waseem et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2025b). By analyzing issue tracking data, our study directly observes the practical issues and root causes that developers encounter, as well as the solutions they employ when building and maintaining LLM-based MAS.

A motivating example: Figure 1 presents a sample GitHub issue (CrewAI issue #2606) from an LLM-based MAS project in which a developer reports a type validation issue where the manager agent passes structured dictionary inputs while the schema expects string values. To ensure consistency, the developer proposes enforcing a JSON message format, thereby highlighting an Orchestration & Execution Issue. Overall, the issue highlights a type mismatch in multi-agent coordination within LLM-based MAS.

Our study aims to identify the issues in developing and using open-source LLM-based MAS and to determine the causes of these issues, as well as possible solutions. With this aim in mind, we formulate three Research Questions (RQs):

  • •

    RQ1: What issues do practitioners face when working on LLM-based MAS?

  • •

    RQ2: What are the underlying causes of the issues in LLM-based MAS?

  • •

    RQ3: What are the potential solutions to address the issues in LLM-based MAS?

To answer RQ1–RQ3, we analyzed the filtered set of 944 GitHub issues to identify the issues reported by practitioners, examine their underlying causes, and the solutions adopted in practice.

Our findings show that: (1) Orchestration & Execution Issue is the most common issue faced by practitioners, (2) Workflow Problem, Tool Integration Problem, and Memory Problem are identified as the most frequent causes of the issues, and (3) Optimize Workflow and Adjust Configuration are the predominant solutions to the issues in LLM-based MAS.

The main contributions of this work are threefold: (1) We identify the key issues that occur during the development of LLM-based MAS projects using the dataset (Rehman et al., 2026) and organize them into a two-level taxonomy to provide a hierarchical understanding of their characteristics. (2) We identify the root causes of these issues and document the corresponding solutions proposed and adopted by practitioners, organizing both into taxonomies for causes and solutions. (3) We establish and analyze the mapping relationships between the identified issues and their underlying causes, as well as between the issues and their associated solutions, to better understand how issues are triggered and addressed in practice.

The rest of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the Research Questions (RQs) and the research methodology employed in this study. Section 3 presents the study results. Section 4 discusses the findings and implications based on the study results. Section 5 discusses the threats to validity. Section 6 reviews the related work, and Section 7 concludes this work along with the directions for future research.

2 Methodology

This study follows a systematic, multi-stage research methodology to investigate the practitioner-reported issues, underlying causes, and corresponding solutions in open-source LLM-based MAS. Based on this objective, we formulate three Research Questions (RQs) to guide the subsequent phases of the study and ensure a structured and reproducible analysis process, as shown in Figure 2. The research process comprises the formulation of RQs in Section 2.1, data collection in Section 2.2, data filtering and labeling in Section 2.3, data extraction in Section 2.4, and data analysis in Section 2.5.

2.1 Research Questions

RQ1: What issues do practitioners face when working on MAS?

Rationale: As stated in Section 1, recent advances in LLMs (Zhao et al., 2023a) have led to a rapid increase in OSS that use LLMs as core components for building intelligent agents (i.e., LLM-based MAS). This RQ aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the issues faced by OSS software engineers while developing MAS. This understanding provides an empirical foundation for identifying the critical challenges that require attention in the design and development of LLM-based MAS. Therefore, identifying and analyzing these practical difficulties is a fundamental first step in this study.

RQ2: What are the underlying causes of the issues in a MAS?

Rationale: Following the identification of issues currently faced by practitioners in RQ1, it is necessary to determine their underlying causes. Identifying these root causes allows this study to provide more practical and actionable recommendations for developing effective, context-specific solutions. Additionally, these insights can inform the ongoing refinement and optimization of both LLM-based MAS and the underlying foundation models.

RQ3: What are the potential solutions to address the issues in MAS?

Rationale: This RQ seeks to understand how OSS practitioners address the challenges encountered during the development and maintenance of LLM-based MAS. Answering this RQ will identify the most commonly adopted solutions within the MAS community and yield a diverse set of practical, practitioner-validated responses to the issues identified in RQ1. By systematically exploring and analyzing these solutions, the study aims to provide actionable guidance for optimizing the design and implementation of LLM-based MAS.

2.2 Data Collection

We collected data for our study from GitHub repositories that clearly mention MAS in their documentation. GitHub is currently the largest platform for hosting OSS projects. In addition, every project on GitHub has an “Issues” page, which provides a platform for users and developers of the project to report issues experienced during development and usage, and to discuss the identification, analysis, and resolution of these issues with other users and developers. In order to thoroughly explore the causes of issues and their potential solutions, we collected all “closed” issues from the repositories of the selected LLM-based MAS.

To ensure comprehensive data collection, we did not set a start date for the data source. The date we performed the data search was November 16, 2025, and we collected all the closed issues created before this date. The first author utilized a keyword-based search approach, using the search terms “Multi-Agent System”, “Multi-Agent LLM”, and “AI Agents” to search across GitHub. Any project that contained these search terms (e.g., in the project description or tags) was retrieved. After obtaining the search results, we found that although many projects include the terms “Multi-Agent System”, “Multi-Agent LLM”, or “AI Agents”, they do not actually implement multi-agent architectures or utilize multiple LLM-based agents as core components. For example, some projects focus on teaching multi-agent concepts without building functional MAS. Therefore, we established the following criteria for selecting open-source LLM-Based MAS projects.

Table 1 summarizes the inclusion and exclusion criteria used in this study. We defined an inclusion criterion (I5) to select projects that utilize multi-agent LLM architectures as core architectural components for their primary functionality. Following established empirical practices (Cai et al., 2025b; Lin et al., 2025), we further applied the inclusion criterion (I1)–(I4) as benchmarks for evaluating project quality, activity, and popularity. By enforcing thresholds on star counts, contributor participation, issue resolution history, and recent update activity, we excluded inactive or unpopular repositories.

We prioritized projects with recent commit activity to ensure they reflect current MAS practices, and we manually verified whether each project explicitly described multi-agent collaboration rather than single-agent LLM usage. In addition, the exclusion criteria (E1) and (E2) were applied to remove educational, tutorial-oriented, or competition-based projects, as well as repositories that only reference multi-agent concepts without implementing actual multi-agent functionality. This selection process ensures that the final dataset is representative of established and actively maintained LLM-based MAS.

After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, we carefully examined the remaining repositories to ensure that they implemented LLM-based MAS and satisfied all selection requirements. Repositories that only partially met the criteria, lacked sufficient project information, or did not provide clear evidence of multi-agent functionality were excluded. Through this screening process, we identified a final set of 21 actively maintained open-source LLM-based MAS projects, which formed the basis of our subsequent analysis. Following the selection criteria, we ultimately included 21 open-source LLM-based MAS (see Table 2) that met our criteria. The domains of the 21 selected LLM-based MAS projects are categorized into six categories (see Table 3). Then, the first author employed web scrapers to collect all the closed issues from these project repositories. In the end, we gathered a total of 22,848 closed issues. Each closed issue was recorded in an MS Excel file. We named each MS Excel file using the convention: “Project Name” + “_” + “Issue Number”.

2.3 Data Filtering and Labeling

We collected closed issues from 21 open-source LLM-based MAS and observed that not all reported issues were relevant to MAS-related problems. For example, some practitioners used issue trackers for community interaction or general inquiries, such as requesting access to a project’s Discord channel Agency-swarm #37, without describing any technical problem in the MAS projects. We also identified issues that were purely single-agent in nature and did not involve multi-agent collaboration, despite being reported in MAS project repositories (e.g., Sdk-python #1435). In addition, we found that the issue labels were often too generic, and relying solely on existing labels could lead to missing relevant information. For example, the multi-agent Orchestration Issue reported in Autogen #6819 was assigned only the generic Bug label, making it difficult to identify through label-based filtering alone.

To address these challenges in filtering and labeling MAS-related issues, we adopted a two-stage mixed approach, combining automated and manual filtering methods to construct a high-quality dataset. This process focused on identifying closed issues that explicitly describe practitioner-reported problems related to MAS. Based on the pilot and formal filtering results in Section 2.3.1 and Section 2.3.2, the final dataset was constructed and subsequently used for data extraction and analysis.

2.3.1 Pilot Data Filtering

We conducted pilot data filtering by randomly selecting 100 closed issues from the collected dataset. The first and second authors independently labeled these issues to minimize potential personal bias. We observed that multi-agent issues were rare only 11 issues were related to real MAS issues, whereas non-multi-agent issues accounted for a relatively large proportion. Therefore, we adopted a mixed approach, combining automated and manual methods for data filtering, to ensure a high-quality dataset for our study. The pilot filtering results were compiled and recorded in MS Excel files (Rehman et al., 2026).

Automated Filtering: We applied a pilot automated filtering approach (He et al., 2025a), following the methodology of prior studies demonstrating the effectiveness of LLM-based evaluation and automated assessment in software engineering tasks (Zhou et al., 2025a; Crupi et al., 2025). We randomly selected 500 issues from the collected 22,848 closed issues and processed them with the DeepSeek-R1 model deployed locally via Ollama, with carefully crafted prompt instructions and iterative refinement to identify MAS-related issues (Montes et al., 2025). Using this approach, we identified 110 MAS-related issues.

Manual Filtering: To ensure dataset quality, we did not fully rely on the LLM; therefore, manual filtering was also conducted. Two human coders, the first and second authors, were involved in this process. They labeled the same sample of 500 issues independently, which contained information related to problems encountered during the development or use of open-source LLM-based MAS. Inter-rater agreement between the two authors was measured using Cohen’s Kappa coefficient (Cohen, 1960), yielding a value of 0.82, which indicates a very high level of labeling consistency between the two authors. Any disagreements in the pilot labeling results were resolved through discussion involving the fourth author to reach a consensus. Finally, 102 out of the 500 closed issues were considered real multi-agent issues.

Evaluation of Automated Filtering: To evaluate the effectiveness and accuracy of the DeepSeek-R1 model, we compared the automated filtering results with those of the manual filtering. Out of the 500 sampled issues, manual filtering labeled 102 multi-agent-related issues, while automated filtering labeled 110 such issues. The comparison between manual and automated labels yielded 452 agreements, where both methods produced consistent labels (i.e., auto=0, manual=0 or auto=1, manual=1), and 48 disagreements, where the labels differed (i.e., auto=1, manual=0 or auto=0, manual=1). We measured the agreement between the automated filtering results and the human annotations. Using this measure, the automated filtering approach achieved an agreement rate of 90.4%. To examine the 48 disagreements, we reviewed the cases where automated filtering labeled an issue as 0 but manual filtering labeled it as 1. In these cases, MAS concepts were not explicitly mentioned, and the relevance to MAS could only be determined from the issue context rather than explicit keywords. As a result, the LLM did not filter these issues as MAS-related issues. For example, Agentscope #489 does not explicitly describe a multi-agent issue, but its relevance to MAS is only clear from the context, not from explicit keywords. Conversely, in cases where automated filtering labeled an issue as 1 but manual filtering labeled it as 0, the issues often contained MAS-related terminology or project components, leading the LLM to filter them as MAS-related issues. However, during manual filtering, they were determined not to clearly describe practitioner-reported MAS-related issues. For example, PraisonAI #234 reports a dependency installation error but uses the term CrewAI, which is a MAS framework. Based on this keyword, the LLM classified it as a MAS-related issue. Similarly, Claude-flow #571 uses the phrase Hive Mind, which refers to MAS functionality, but it is actually a release announcement describing bug fixes and improvements rather than a practitioner-reported issue.

2.3.2 Formal Data Filtering

We conducted formal data filtering on the collected 22,848 closed issues. In this process, we excluded the issues not related to our study. We selected projects in which LLM-based MAS is a core component, and we kept those issues related to the problems that practitioners encountered during the development and use of open-source LLM-based MAS. As observed in the pilot study (see Section 2.3.1), the proportion of real MAS issues among the collected 22,848 closed issues was relatively low. Therefore, we adopted a mixed approach, combining automated and manual methods to construct a high-quality dataset. Accordingly, we first applied automated filtering to all 22,848 collected closed issues using the DeepSeek-R1 model deployed locally via Ollama, with carefully crafted prompt instructions and iterative refinement (Montes et al., 2025), to identify MAS-related issues (He et al., 2025a). This automated filtering identified 2,335 multi-agent-related closed issues. To ensure dataset quality, we did not fully rely on the LLM; therefore, manual filtering was also conducted. The first author was involved in manually reviewing the results of the automated filtering to ensure data quality. Any disagreements in the formal data filtering results were resolved through discussion involving the fourth author to reach a consensus. Finally, 944 out of the 22,848 closed issues were considered real multi-agent issues. The source projects of the closed issues in the final dataset are presented in Table 4. In addition, the distribution of the duration from issue opening to closing for the closed issues in the final dataset is shown in Figure 3. The results of the formal data filtering were compiled and recorded in MS Excel files (Rehman et al., 2026).

2.4 Data Extraction

To answer the three RQs presented in Section 2.1, we defined a set of data items for data extraction, as shown in Table 5. The data items D1–D3 are used to extract information about issues, underlying causes, and solutions that address these issues, corresponding to RQ1–RQ3, respectively. These data items are extracted from different parts of the collected closed issues, including the title, description, and discussion. To ensure the accuracy of the data extraction results and the validity of the subsequent data analysis, we decided to conduct the data extraction manually. In addition, the dataset size is relatively small, making manual data extraction feasible. The details of the pilot and formal data extraction procedures are presented in Section 2.4.1 and Section 2.4.2, respectively.

2.4.1 Pilot Data Extraction

We randomly selected 100 closed issues from our filtered dataset. The first author then independently performed pilot data extraction on these issues. The results indicate that all three data items (see Table 5) can be extracted from our dataset. Based on the pilot extraction results, we reached a consensus and defined the following rules for formal data extraction. (1) In principle, only one issue is extracted from each closed issue; if multiple issues can be extracted, we record the first issue discussed. (2) If there are multiple causes mentioned in a closed issue, we record all the causes of the issue extracted in the former step, which are identified by the reporter and the development team. (3) Similarly, if there are multiple solutions mentioned in a closed issue, we record all the solutions identified by the reporter and the development team that can address the issue extracted in the former step.

2.4.2 Formal Data Extraction

Following the pilot phase, the first author independently performed the formal data extraction based on the items defined in Table 5. Any ambiguities encountered during the data extraction process were resolved through discussions with the fourth author to ensure consistency. After completing the data extraction, the second and fourth authors reviewed the results and discussed them with the first author to resolve inconsistencies and reach a consensus. Both authors further conducted multiple rounds of review and refinement to ensure the accuracy of the final dataset. The final results were compiled and recorded in an MS Excel file (Rehman et al., 2026).

During the formal data extraction, we identified 16 closed issues that contained multiple problems within a single GitHub issue report (e.g., CrewAI #3918). In accordance with our predefined criteria in Section 2.4.1, we included only the first reported problem along with its corresponding causes and solutions. We also observed that not all closed issues contained clearly extractable information (i.e., causes or solutions). In some cases, the discussion was too vague to identify specific causes or solutions, while in others, issues were automatically closed due to inactivity, low priority, or high complexity, making it difficult to extract information.

2.5 Data Analysis

After completing the data extraction, we performed data analysis to address the three RQs formulated in Section 2.1. We applied the Open Coding and Constant Comparison methods, which are widely used in Grounded Theory for qualitative analysis in software engineering research (Stol et al., 2016). Open Coding represents the initial stage of analysis, where researchers systematically examine the text to identify key concepts and categories, assigning descriptive codes to each element. Constant Comparison follows as a refinement stage, in which researchers iteratively compare new data with previously coded data to adjust and integrate categories based on their similarities and differences.

The steps in our data analysis are as follows: (1) The first author meticulously read through the text of each closed issue and assigned descriptive codes that succinctly summarize the core themes according to the three RQs (see Table 5). For example, Smolagents #1353 was coded as ‘‘Agent Tool Registration Failure’’, which indicates an error caused by improper agent integration. (2) The first author compared commonalities and differences among codes. Following a bottom-up approach, identical or similar codes were grouped into higher-level types and categories. For example, the code from Smolagents #1353, along with similar instances, constituted a Tool Invocation Error type under the broader Tool Issue category. (3) When uncertainties about code descriptions arose, the first author discussed them with the second and fourth authors to reach a consensus. Due to the iterative nature of constant comparison, the initial results underwent several modifications. (4) The fourth author reviewed and verified the initial analysis. Subsequently, all other authors reviewed the final results and made further refinements to improve the accuracy and consistency of the analysis. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion; after resolving 29 conflicts in issue categories, 24 in cause categories, and 22 in solution categories, we obtained the final data analysis results.

3 Results and Interpretation

We present the findings of the three RQs and discuss their implications. We introduce a two-stage classification for the Issue, Cause, and Solution taxonomies, where an Issue refers to a problem reported by practitioners in LLM-based MAS, a Cause represents the underlying reason for the problem, and a Solution describes the approach used to resolve it. The taxonomies consist of categories and types, and brief descriptions of each type are provided under the corresponding category. To demonstrate the relationships among issues, causes, and solutions, we present mappings between Issue and Cause categories, as well as between Issue and Solution categories. It should be noted that only closed issues for which a solution has been extracted are included in the issue solution mapping. Similarly, only closed issues for which a cause has been extracted are included in the issue cause mapping. The taxonomy of issues in the final dataset is shown in Figure 4, while the distribution of their closure durations is presented in Figure 3. To further interpret these findings, we identify key patterns in the results and examine their implications for issues, causes, and solutions in LLM-based MAS.

3.1 Category of Issues (RQ1)

Figure 4 shows the taxonomy of the closed issues extracted from the dataset. The results show that Orchestration & Execution Issue (22.0%) is the most frequent category reported by practitioners in open-source LLM-based MAS projects, followed by Memory & State Management Issue (14.7%) and Feature Request (13.2%). Implementation Issue (10.6%) also represents a notable portion of the dataset. The remaining categories each account for less than 10%, including Tool Issue (9.2%), Integration Issue (6.7%), Role Issue (3.8%), Environment & Configuration Issue (3.5%), Output Issue (3.1%), Documentation Issue (2.8%), Communication Issue (2.6%), Performance Issue (2.0%), Model Issue (1.6%), Compatibility Issue (1.4%), Error Handling Issue (1.3%), Task Management Issue (1.2%), and Security Issue (0.3%).

3.1.1 Orchestration & Execution Issue

(22.0%) Orchestration & Execution Issue refers to problems arising from agent orchestration and LLM-based execution control during runtime in the development and use of open-source LLM-based MAS. This category comprises the following ten issue types.

  • •

    Coordination & Handoff Issue refers to issues in interaction and task transfer between agents in LLM-based MAS. These issues usually arise when agents fail to properly coordinate or hand off tasks, leading to delays, duplication, unexpected outputs, or incomplete execution. For example, a practitioner reported that “sub-agent could not correctly transfer to root agent and call the MCP tool” (Adk-python #1039).

  • •

    Control Flow Error refers to issues where the execution order between agents or tasks does not behave as expected. These issues include incorrect sequencing, unexpected loop behavior, or disrupted execution flow, which may lead to incorrect outputs, execution failure, or early termination. For example, a practitioner reported that “SequentialAgent doesn’t execute sub-agents after the first one” (Adk-python #573).

  • •

    Infinite Execution Loop refers to issues where agents become trapped in continuous execution without a valid termination condition. These issues arise from missing termination logic, weak control, or poor coordination, leading to resource waste and incomplete workflows. For example, a practitioner reported that “agentic parallelization with different agents/tasks: tasks repeat in a loop, aggregator never runs, process never completes” (PraisonAI #864).

  • •

    Termination Failure refers to issues where execution continues even after a valid termination condition is met. These issues result from incorrect termination signaling or inconsistent stopping conditions, causing workflows to run longer than necessary. For example, a practitioner reported that “termination on the receiving agent doesn’t terminate the program” (Autogen #1919).

  • •

    Premature Termination refers to issues where execution stops before all agents complete their tasks. These issues arise from incorrect orchestration, early stopping, or faulty propagation, resulting in partial workflow execution. For example, a practitioner reported that “multi-agent chain stops at first agent without executing others in v2.2.7” (Flowise #4321).

  • •

    Resource Limitation refers to issues where LLM-based MAS experience resource conflicts, shared tool contention, or time constraints. These issues result in execution hangs, failures, or early termination. For example, a practitioner reported that “Claude-Flow swarm command consistently times out due to resource conflicts between the swarm execution and active Claude Code sessions” (Claude-flow #59).

  • •

    Agent Selection Issue refers to issues where the routing or delegation mechanism fails to identify and assign the most appropriate specialized agent for a given task. These issues lead to incorrect agent selection or failed agent delegation decisions, resulting in incorrect or failed task execution. For example, a practitioner reported that “manager llm doesn’t seem to be working properly and does not seem to delegate the query to other agents” (CrewAI #1503).

  • •

    Agent Design Issue refers to issues where agent architectural design, data flow, or inter-agent communication is difficult to define or implement in LLM-based MAS. These issues lead to challenges in chaining agents, handling structured data, or maintaining consistency across agent boundaries, resulting in orchestration errors or workflow breakdowns. For example, a practitioner reported that “passing information between 2 agents is cumbersome” (Agno #2391).

  • •

    Context Loss refers to issues where runtime contextual information (e.g., domain, task constraints, or user instructions) is not properly propagated between agents during execution. Agents ignore or revert to default values instead of following the intended context, leading to incorrect or unexpected behavior. For example, a practitioner reported that “agents failed to consistently follow the specified domain context during multi-agent execution, repeatedly using the wrong domain example.com” (PraisonAI #289).

  • •

    Concurrency Issue refers to issues where shared state is not properly managed when multiple agents execute in parallel. These issues arise when actions from different agents are processed in an unexpected order, potentially leading to inconsistent or incomplete context, runtime errors, or unstable behavior. For example, a practitioner reported that “when running multiple agents in parallel, events coming from different agents can interleave” (Adk-python #2404).

Interpretation: The high proportion of Orchestration & Execution Issue indicates that runtime coordination is the main challenge in LLM-based MAS. Coordination & Handoff Issue (62) and Control Flow Errors (40) are the most frequent types of issues in this category. Coordination & Handoff Issue reflect failures in task transfer between agents, while Control Flow Error indicate incorrect or unstable execution ordering. Overall, most issues arise from weak coordination between agents rather than limitations in individual agents. This indicates a gap between theoretical multi-agent design and practical execution reliability. The findings highlight orchestration as a key bottleneck and the need for better execution control and coordination mechanisms in future LLM-based MAS.

3.1.2 Memory & State Management Issue

(14.7%) Memory & State Management Issue refers to issues in storing, updating, and propagating memory, state, or intermediate information across agents during execution. Practitioners encounter these challenges during the development and use of LLM-based multi-agent OSS. This category encompasses the following six types.

  • •

    Context Loss refers to issues where persistent state or shared memory is not properly maintained or retrieved across agents during execution. Contextual information stored at higher levels is not consistently propagated or is reinitialized instead of being reused, causing agents to lose access to previously established states and leading to inconsistent or incorrect behavior across execution steps. For example, a practitioner reported that “team shared context is lost whenever moving on to subsequent agent” (Agno #3254).

  • •

    State Inconsistency refers to issues where shared state or intermediate outputs are not consistently visible, synchronized, or aligned across agents during execution. State updates are not reliably propagated, or different agents access different versions of the same state due to timing or synchronization issues, causing agents to operate on inconsistent state views, leading to unreliable or divergent execution behavior. For example, a practitioner reported that “the second agent is often unable to see items stored in the state of the previous agent” (Adk-python #1119).

  • •

    State Persistence Failure refers to issues where stored state or session-level information is not correctly initialized, preserved, or made accessible across agents during execution. State is not properly bound to session identifiers, or stored information becomes unavailable during runtime despite being explicitly defined, preventing agents from retrieving previously stored session state and leading to incomplete or incorrect execution. For example, a practitioner reported that “team_session_state not initialized when session_id is provided” (Agno #3799).

  • •

    Retrieval Failure refers to issues where previously stored state, memory entries, or checkpoints cannot be reliably accessed during execution, even if they exist in the system. Agents fail to retrieve the required previous state, leading to incomplete workflow progression or reduced system reliability. For example, a practitioner reported that “in a sequential agent workflow, the system randomly fails to retrieve stored checkpoints” (Flowise #3859).

  • •

    Context Overflow refers to issues where accumulated contextual information exceeds the effective input or memory capacity of the system during multi-agent execution. Multiple agents continuously contribute information without filtering or compression, making the input context excessively large and leading to degraded performance or loss of relevant signals during reasoning. For example, a practitioner reported that “a single agent needs to store information from multiple agents, which can lead to excessively long token lengths in the input for large models” (Agentscope #637).

  • •

    State Loss refers to issues where parts of the generated or updated state are not retained in the final execution outcome. In multi-agent or parallel workflows, intermediate state updates are overwritten, dropped, or not properly merged during aggregation, causing some agent contributions to be missing from the final system state and resulting in incomplete or partial execution results. For example, a practitioner reported that “state updates from parallel agent calls were not correctly aggregated, causing some agent contributions to be missing from the final session state” (Adk-python #1153).

Interpretation: The high proportion of Memory & State Management Issue indicates that state handling is a critical challenge in LLM-based MAS. Context Loss (42) and State Inconsistency (36) are the most frequently reported issues, showing a consistent pattern of unreliable state propagation across agents. There is a clear gap between the designed memory abstractions and their actual behavior in execution. This highlights the need for reliable state management and memory propagation mechanisms in future MAS.

3.1.3 Feature Request

(13.2%) Feature Request refers to practitioner-driven requests for new capabilities or enhancements in LLM-based MAS. These requests typically highlight gaps between existing system capabilities and real-world application needs. This category encompasses the following five types.

  • •

    Extensibility & Customization refers to requests for extending system flexibility to support custom configurations, models, or agent-specific behaviors in LLM-based MAS. For example, a practitioner requested “ textit Is it possible to define multiple (local) LLMs in the config.yaml for different agents?” (MetaGPT #1266).

  • •

    Communication & Data Flow refers to requests for improving how information is transmitted, streamed, or exposed across agents and system components in LLM-based MAS. These requests typically arise when intermediate outputs or interactions are not visible or are delayed during execution. For example, a practitioner requested “a way to output or stream AgentFlows like Chat inside Flowise app” (Flowise #2838).

  • •

    Monitoring & Debugging refers to requests for improving visibility into agent behavior, execution steps, and system-level activities in LLM-based MAS. These requests typically arise when practitioners cannot observe how agents make decisions or interact with tools and data during execution. For example, a practitioner requested “observability of agents’ actions taken, tools used, and data accessed” (AutoGen #2423).

  • •

    Framework Limitation refers to requests in multi-agent frameworks where certain capabilities or design requirements are not directly supported by the existing system design or API. These requests typically arise when the framework only supports simple sequential or instruction-based workflows, thereby limiting more structured orchestration designs. For example, a practitioner requested support for advanced orchestration patterns: “The agent team API cannot handle complicated workflows or hierarchical multi-agent patterns” (Agno #2209).

  • •

    Performance & Scalability refers to requests aimed at improving execution speed, parallelism, and system throughput in multi-agent frameworks. These requests typically arise when current systems do not efficiently support large-scale agent execution or real-time control over running processes. For example, a practitioner proposed “parallel agent spawning to improve execution speed and support real-time query control in multi-agent workflows” (Claude-flow #781).

Interpretation: The Feature Request category shows that practitioners mainly focus on extending the capabilities of existing multi-agent frameworks. A clear pattern emerges in Extensibility & Customization (57) and Communication & Data Flow (27), where users request more flexible configurations and support for advanced design capabilities not directly available in existing frameworks. Overall, these findings indicate that current MAS frameworks are functional but still limited in flexibility, leading practitioners to request more adaptable and extensible system designs.

3.1.4 Implementation Issue

(10.6%) Implementation Issue refers to issues arising from incorrect or incomplete implementation in LLM-based MAS during development or runtime. This category encompasses the following seven types.

  • •

    Execution Logic Error refers to issues arising from incorrect or unintended execution behavior caused by flaws in implementation logic during runtime in LLM-based MAS. Function calls, control flow, or internal execution mechanisms do not behave as intended, leading to runtime errors or incorrect execution paths despite a correct intended design. For example, a practitioner reported that when an agent is copied, method references become mismatched: “the copied version of the BoardAgent causes a KeyError when accessing hook_lists[self.process_all_messages]” (AutoGen #1706).

  • •

    Correctness Issue refers to issues where the system produces factually incorrect, logically inconsistent, or semantically invalid results during execution in LLM-based MAS. Agent reasoning or intermediate computations deviate from expected functional behavior despite successful execution, resulting in wrong answers, miscalculations, or flawed decisions even when the output format is correct. For example, a practitioner reported that the system returns incorrect stock prices in a multi-agent setup: “multi-agent framework not working as expected, issue with finance lib as well internally” (Agno #1700).

  • •

    Dependency Conflict refers to issues where different framework or library versions lead to incompatible behaviors in LLM-based MAS. These issues arise when updates in dependencies modify core execution logic or agent interaction mechanisms, causing regressions in previously working workflows or system failures. For example, a practitioner reported that a version update breaks the group chat speaker selection logic: “Autogen Studio GroupChatWorkflow not working on pyautogen==0.2.13 but working on pyautogen==0.2.10” (AutoGen #1693).

  • •

    Parameter Configuration Error refers to issues where incorrect or inconsistent parameter passing, or misconfiguration in setup, leads to unexpected behavior in LLM-based MAS during execution. These issues typically arise when input parameters are not properly propagated across agents, tools, or execution modes under different runtime settings, causing the system to execute successfully but fail to correctly utilize required inputs, resulting in incomplete behavior. For example, a practitioner reported that enabling streaming causes the files argument to be lost during execution: “Files parameter not passed to tools when using team streaming” (Agno #5121).

  • •

    Missing Attribute/Parameter refers to implementation issues where required attributes or parameters are missing or incorrectly defined in data models or execution objects in LLM-based MAS. Framework components evolve, but dependent modules or logging/processing layers are not updated accordingly, leading to attribute mismatches during runtime. For example, a practitioner reported that “AttributeError: ‘Message’ object has no attribute ‘params’” (Adk-python #2930).

  • •

    Class Issue refers to implementation issues where class types are not properly registered, recognized, or handled during runtime in LLM-based MAS. Custom or extended class types (including structured outputs) may not be supported by existing runtime components, leading to execution errors. For example, a practitioner reported that custom structured message classes are not recognized by the group chat runtime: “agent’s StructuredMessage class is not registered in GroupChat” (AutoGen #6983).

  • •

    Agent Execution Issue refers to issues where agents do not follow the intended execution strategy (e.g., parallelism, scheduling, or control flow) during runtime. The orchestration layer may enforce unintended sequential processing, leading to agents executing in a different order than expected. For example, a practitioner reported that “graph nodes execute sequentially instead of parallel” (Sdk-python #478).

Interpretation: The substantial proportion of Implementation Issue indicates that correct runtime behavior is a critical challenge in LLM-based MAS. Execution Logic Error (29) and Correctness Issue (20) highlight a consistent pattern of faulty execution flow and incorrect system behavior. There is a clear gap between intended system design and its implementation, as implementation flaws lead to incorrect execution behavior, dependency conflicts, parameter misconfigurations, and other runtime issues in LLM-based MAS.

3.1.5 Tool Issue

(9.2%) Tool Issue refers to issues arising from incorrect integration, configuration, or usage of external tools in LLM-based MAS. This category encompasses the following four types.

  • •

    Tool Execution Failure refers to issues that arise when tools fail during the runtime execution of LLM-based MAS. Tool invocation mechanisms or execution environments are improperly handled, leading to crashes or incomplete execution despite correct setup. For example, a practitioner reported that improper async handling causes a runtime error when invoking tools in a group chat: “GroupChat cannot run with MCP tool call (async await issue)” (Ag2 #1763).

  • •

    Tool Invocation Error refers to issues where tools are incorrectly invoked during execution in LLM-based MAS. Function names, mappings, or invocation logic are improperly configured, leading to calls to invalid or non-existent tools and failure to execute the intended functions. For example, a practitioner reported that missing function mappings cause incorrect tool selection: “AutoGen tries to call non-existent functions that are the names of agents” (AutoGen #781).

  • •

    Tool Selection Error refers to issues where agents improperly select or access tools that are not intended for them in LLM-based MAS. These issues typically arise when tool access boundaries are not properly defined in the multi-agent group configuration or when tools assigned to one agent become available to other agents, allowing these agents to use tools beyond their intended scope. For example, a practitioner reported that an agent uses tools registered for another agent due to shared group context: “Why agent can use tools from another agent in autogen” (AutoGen #4399).

  • •

    Parameter Configuration Error refers to issues arising from incorrect or incompatible parameter definitions in tool schemas within LLM-based MAS. The selected tool is correct, but the provided inputs do not align with the expected tool schema in terms of structure, type, or format, leading to validation failures before tool execution. For example, a practitioner reported that “the manager agent passes dictionary values where the delegation tool schema expects strings” (CrewAI #2606).

Interpretation: The Tool Issue category highlights key challenges in LLM-based MAS related to tool usage during execution. The most common issues include Tool Execution Failure (41) and Tool Invocation Error (28). These findings indicate that issues primarily arise from runtime breakdowns and incorrect tool selection in multi-agent settings, reflecting a gap between intended tool behavior and actual system execution.

3.1.6 Integration Issue

(6.7%) Integration Issues refer to issues related to the interaction and compatibility between different components in LLM-based MAS that practitioners encounter while developing and using these MAS. This category encompasses the following five types.

  • •

    API Integration Failure refers to issues where external APIs or service-based models fail to integrate properly within LLM-based MAS. Integration issues between certain APIs or live services during execution result in runtime errors, thereby limiting communication between agents and external services. For example, a practitioner reported that live API constraints prevent the proper integration of sub-agent functionality: “Live Event, Live API stuffs cannot use sub-agent” (Adk-python #491).

  • •

    Parameter Misconfiguration refers to issues where parameter definitions used during the integration of external models or APIs do not align with the expected schema in LLM-based MAS. The selected model or service is correct, but the parameters passed across system components are improperly structured, missing required fields, or incompatible with the API specification. For example, a practitioner reported that misconfigured tool parameters cause schema validation errors: “Gemini models in agent mode giving error 400 invalid argument” (Continue #6121).

  • •

    Dependency Conflict refers to issues in which incompatible or mismatched library dependencies hinder the successful integration of components in LLM-based MAS. Different system environments rely on conflicting package versions or unsupported dependency combinations. For example, a practitioner reported that dependency incompatibilities lead to integration failures during deployment due to serialization errors: “GroupChatWorkflow breaks after upgrading from pyautogen==0.2.10 to 0.2.13 due to incompatible dependency behavior” (Autogen #1693).

  • •

    Interface Compatibility Problem refers to issues arising from incompatibility between different interfaces or execution environments in LLM-based MAS. The same agentic workflow behaves correctly in a local or direct execution environment but fails when integrated with external interfaces such as web sockets, IO streams, or service-based communication layers. For example, a practitioner reported that a group chat system fails to execute function calls when running through a WebSocket integration, despite working correctly in a direct environment: “Group-chat will not call function when using IOStream” (AutoGen #2824).

  • •

    Framework Integration Issue refers to issues where external multi-agent frameworks or libraries fail to integrate correctly within LLM-based MAS. Developers combine different agent frameworks or extend reference implementations, but runtime behavior breaks due to missing framework-specific configurations, incompatible abstractions, or incorrect usage of required components. For example, a practitioner reported that a SemanticKernel-based multi-agent setup fails when adapting a reference group-chat implementation, resulting in runtime exceptions: “Write sample based on SemanticKernel with content copied from Example04_Dynamic_GroupChat_Coding_Task, can’t work” (AutoGen #2688).

Interpretation: The Integration Issue category highlights key challenges in LLM-based MAS related to integrating external APIs, frameworks, and system components. The most common issues include API Integration Failure (36) and Parameter Misconfiguration (8). Overall, these findings indicate that even when components are present and accessible, failures mainly arise from incorrect integration and mismatched assumptions across the system. Overall, these findings indicate that integration issues stem primarily from incompatibilities and configuration mismatches between external components and the MAS.

3.1.7 Role Issue

(3.8%) Role Issue refers to issues related to incorrect or unclear role assignment in LLM-based MAS, where agents fail to consistently follow their intended roles during execution. This category encompasses the following two types.

  • •

    Role Assignment Error refers to issues where LLM-based MAS fail to correctly assign or evaluate roles during execution. The role assignment mechanism or routing logic does not produce valid or sufficient role decisions, leading to execution failure or inability to proceed with multi-agent coordination. For example, a practitioner reported that “role assignment fails when the system receives insufficient compatibility scores for the user role, preventing the multi-agent process from proceeding” (CAMEL #419).

  • •

    Role Misalignment refers to issues where LLM-based MAS store incorrect role labels in logs or chat history, even when the execution flow is correct. Message handling or logging mechanisms record wrong role tags (e.g., user messages recorded as assistant), leading to inconsistencies between actual agent behavior and the recorded system state. For example, a practitioner reported that messages from a user proxy agent are incorrectly recorded as assistant in the chat history: “Wrong role set in group chat” (AutoGen #3009).

Interpretation: The Role Issue category highlights key challenges in LLM-based MAS related to correct role assignment and role labeling. These issues comprise Role Assignment Error (30) and Role Misalignment (6). Overall, role-related problems affect both role behavior during execution and role recording in logs, leading to inconsistencies between actual agent behavior and stored role information.

3.1.8 Environment & Configuration Issue

(3.5%) Environment & Configuration Issue refers to issues arising from incorrect setup, dependency management, or runtime environment configuration in LLM-based MAS, where agents fail to initialize or execute correctly. This category encompasses the following four types.

  • •

    Dependency Conflict refers to issues where incompatible library or package versions in the execution environment prevent proper initialization or execution of LLM-based MAS. These runtime environment mismatches lead to runtime failures such as missing attributes or import errors, even when the system logic is correctly implemented. For example, a practitioner reported that a version mismatch between autogen_studio and autogen_agentchat causes a missing attribute error during team initialization: “Type object team has no attribute load_component with AutoGen Studio v0.4.0.4” (AutoGen #5319).

  • •

    Parameter Configuration Error refers to issues where parameter configuration is incorrectly structured or not properly mapped to target agents or nodes in the current execution environment in LLM-based MAS. Runtime parameter overrides fail when schema mismatches, invalid formatting, or incorrect node identifiers, leading to execution errors or ignored settings despite correct system logic. For example, a practitioner reported that structured override configurations for sequential agents and LLM nodes cause runtime errors: “Can’t override data for sequential agents” (Flowise #3240).

  • •

    Environment Misconfiguration refers to issues where LLM-based MAS fail when incorrect or incompatible deployment environment settings, such as networking rules, service exposure, or runtime constraints in cloud or containerized setups. These issues prevent agents from accessing external services or internal APIs, leading to connection failures despite correct system logic. For example, a practitioner reported that agent creation fails because of Kubernetes networking restrictions that block access to external AI endpoints: “AI agents fail to create due to Kubernetes networking constraints” (Activepieces #9038).

  • •

    API Integration Failure refers to issues where external APIs or tool interfaces fail to operate correctly due to environmental configuration constraints in LLM-based MAS. Incorrect lifecycle management or missing integration handling between the agent framework and external API services prevents agents from accessing API-based tools despite correct system logic. For example, a practitioner reported that MCP tool connections fail inside a FastAPI-mounted application because of improper lifecycle handling of the API interface: “mounting AgentOS app on existing FastAPI prevents MCP tools connection” (Agno #4958).

Interpretation: The Environment & Configuration Issue category highlights key challenges in LLM-based MAS related to deployment setup, dependency management, and external service integration. The most common issues include Dependency Conflict (9) and Parameter Configuration Error (9). Overall, these findings indicate that environment & configuration issues can prevent agents from initializing, communicating, or executing correctly within LLM-based MAS.

3.1.9 Output Issue

(3.1%) Output Issue refers to issues related to incorrect, incomplete, or malformed outputs generated by LLM-based MAS during execution that practitioners encounter while developing and using these systems. This category encompasses the following three types.

  • •

    Incomplete Response refers to issues where LLM-based MAS return only a subset of the expected output, omitting intermediate results, agent-level responses, or other information from the execution process. This reduces transparency and makes it difficult to understand how the final answer was produced. For example, a practitioner reported that only the final conclusion is returned through the API while intermediate worker outputs are hidden: “API of Agentflows not displaying the answers of each worker” (Flowise #2706).

  • •

    Output Inaccuracy refers to issues where LLM-based MAS generate outputs containing unintended formatting artifacts or structural tokens in the final response, such as extra symbols, wrappers, or formatting noise not intended in the output format. This makes the output unsuitable for direct use or downstream processing. For example, a practitioner reported that “triple backticks (“‘) are appended unexpectedly at the end of crew output responses” (CrewAI #2105).

  • •

    Output Inconsistency refers to issues where LLM-based MAS produce inconsistent or unstable outputs under the same input conditions, even when the prompt, model, and configuration remain unchanged. These inconsistencies may arise from variations in multi-agent coordination, task decomposition, or sequential execution, leading to differences in the generated outputs. For example, a practitioner reported that “Crew fails to deliver the same output as ChatGPT given the same prompt and model” (CrewAI #1024).

Interpretation: The Output Issue category highlights key challenges in LLM-based MAS related to the completeness, correctness, and reliability of generated outputs. The most common issues include Incomplete Response (12) and Output Inaccuracy (10). Overall, these findings indicate that incomplete, malformed, and inconsistent outputs can reduce the usability and reliability of responses generated by LLM-based MAS.

3.1.10 Documentation Issue

(2.8%) Documentation Issue refers to issues related to missing, unclear, or incorrect documentation in LLM-based MAS. This category encompasses the following two types.

  • •

    Unclear Documentation refers to issues where system documentation is inconsistent, ambiguous, or incorrect, leading to confusion during development and usage of LLM-based MAS. Documentation-related information such as agent and tool descriptions, usage instructions, or multi-agent workflows may not align with the actual implementation in LLM-based MAS. For example, a practitioner reported that documentation references outdated tool prefixes, causing naming confusion: “confusing MCP Tool References - mcp_ruv-swarm vs mcp_claude-flow” (Claude-flow #160).

  • •

    Missing Documentation refers to issues where required information, commands, or usage details are not properly documented in LLM-based MAS. causing confusion during the development and execution of LLM-based MAS. For example, a practitioner reported that “the documentation lacked examples and guidance for the new multi-agent setup using AgentTool” (Adk-Python #1608).

Interpretation: The Documentation Issue category highlights the challenges in LLM-based MAS related to the clarity and completeness of system documentation. These issues include Unclear Documentation (14) and Missing Documentation (12). Overall, these findings indicate that documentation issues reflect a gap between the system and its supporting documentation in LLM-based MAS.

3.1.11 Communication Issue

(2.6%) Communication Issue refers to issues related to interaction, message exchange, and information flow between agents in LLM-based MAS that practitioners encounter while developing and using these systems. This category encompasses the following four types.

  • •

    Message Format Error refers to issues where messages exchanged between agents are incorrectly structured or violate the expected communication protocol (e.g., JSON schema, role fields, or message format), causing failures in inter-agent communication or message processing. For example, a practitioner reported that an entry-point agent sends malformed messages to other agents, requiring a structured format: “Entry point agent occasionally sends incorrect or malformed information when communicating with other agents” (Agency-Swarm #175).

  • •

    Connection Issue refers to issues where communication between agents fails when network or connectivity problems occur, such as network errors, incorrect endpoints, or infrastructure constraints, preventing information exchange and coordinated task execution. For example, a practitioner reported that inter-agent communication fails due to a network error: “A2A inter-agent communication failure due to network/proxy connectivity problem” (Adk-python #2384).

  • •

    Role Assignment Issue refers to issues where agent roles are incorrectly assigned during inter-agent communication, leading to misinterpretation of context by downstream agents and incorrect outputs. For example, a practitioner reported that: “incorrect role assignment in multi-agent mode causes context misinterpretation” (Adk-python #1748).

  • •

    Message Transmission Failure refers to issues where messages or events are not properly transmitted between agents or system components, leading to incomplete information flow. In such cases, communication signals (e.g., intermediate messages) fail to propagate across system. For example, a practitioner reported that a sub-agent successfully executes a tool, but the corresponding event is not transmitted to the frontend: “Sub-agent tool execution event fails to propagate to the frontend” (Agno #3435).

Interpretation: The Communication Issue category highlights key challenges in LLM-based MAS related to message exchange, connectivity, and interaction between agents. The most common issues include Message Format Error (12) and Connection Issue (6). Overall, these findings indicate that incorrect message structuring, communication failures, and network constraints can disrupt information exchange and interaction between agents in LLM-based MAS.

3.1.12 Performance Issue

(2.0%) Performance Issue refers to issues related to execution efficiency, latency, and resource utilization in LLM-based MAS. This category encompasses the following two types.

  • •

    Inefficient Execution refers to issues where LLM-based MAS use resources inefficiently during task execution, leading to redundant processing and increased computational or time overhead, such as when unnecessary agents or processes are involved in task execution. For example, a practitioner reported that: “GroupChat keeps calling all the available agents and doesn’t stop even after output from one agent is generated” (AutoGen #1464).

  • •

    Response Delay refers to issues where LLM-based MAS experience high latency during execution, tool invocation, or response generation. Delays between key stages (e.g., model callbacks, tool calls, or agent communication) result in slow system responsiveness and reduced performance. For example, a practitioner reported that “high latency occurs between agent callbacks and tool invocation during multi-agent execution” (Adk-python #1566).

Interpretation: The Performance Issue category highlights key challenges in LLM-based MAS related to execution efficiency and response latency. The issues include Inefficient Execution (9) and Response Delay (9). Overall, these findings indicate that redundant processing and execution delays can reduce the efficiency and responsiveness of LLM-based MAS.

3.1.13 Model Issue

(1.6%) Model Issue refers to issues arising from model behavior and model-level limitations in LLM-based MAS. This category encompasses the following two types.

  • •

    Message Format Mismatch refers to issues where agents generate outputs in a format that is incompatible with the system’s expected structured output interface. For example, a practitioner reported that the model returns responses in an incorrect object format instead of a properly structured string: “Sequential agents with anthropic return the response as an array of strings instead of the expected string format” (Flowise #3792).

  • •

    API Compatibility Issue refers to issues where LLM-based MAS are incompatible with specific model API requirements or provider constraints during model API integration. Model providers enforce strict API rules that may conflict with MAS design, leading to execution failures despite correct system implementation. For example, a practitioner reported that Anthropic’s API enforces strict role-alternation rules that are incompatible with the system’s conversation structure: “Anthropic Claude rejects sequential multi-agent messages because its API requires alternating user and assistant roles” (Flowise #3147).

Interpretation: The Model Issue category highlights challenges in LLM-based MAS related to model response formatting and platform-specific constraints. The issues include Message Format Mismatch (12) and API Compatibility Issue (3). Overall, these findings indicate that model issues arise from mismatches between model outputs, API requirements, and MAS communication requirements.

3.1.14 Compatibility Issue

(1.4%) Compatibility Issue refers to issues related to version mismatches and incompatibilities between different components or frameworks in LLM-based MAS. This category encompasses the following two types.

  • •

    Interface Type Mismatch refers to issues where LLM-based MAS produce outputs that do not follow the expected data structures defined by external systems or the expected output formats of model APIs. This leads to violations of required constraints in message content types, field formats, or nested structures. For example, a practitioner reported that “sub-agent execution produced array-based content instead of the string format required by the Ollama API” (Adk-python #376).

  • •

    API Compatibility Issue refers to issues where LLM-based MAS fail to comply with provider-specific API requirements. The request sent to the API does not meet required constraints, leading to runtime rejection despite correct system design. For example, a practitioner reported that “crewAI sends conversation messages to WatsonX (IBM’s AI platform) that do not conform to the API’s required user/assistant role sequence” (CrewAI #1619).

Interpretation: The Compatibility Issue category highlights challenges in LLM-based MAS related to interface and protocol-level constraints during integration with external services. The issues include Interface Type Mismatch (10) and API Compatibility Issue (3). Overall, these findings indicate that compatibility issues arise from violations of external interface schemas and provider-specific conversation rules, leading to integration breakdowns despite correct system design.

3.1.15 Error Handling Issue

(1.3%) Error Handling Issue refers to issues related to failure detection, exception handling, and recovery mechanisms in LLM-based MAS. This category encompasses the following two types.

  • •

    Unhandled Exception refers to failures where LLM-based MAS do not properly handle runtime exceptions during execution. These issues arise when variables, inputs, or intermediate states are not correctly defined or passed, which leads to unexpected execution failures. For example, a practitioner reported that “MetaGPT’s ActionNode.fill function raises an UnboundLocalError when the local variable context is referenced before assignment” (MetaGPT #1839).

  • •

    Recovery Failure refers to failures where LLM-based MAS are unable to properly restore or correct system state after an error occurs. This happens because partial execution results are not rolled back or cleared. This results in inconsistent system states despite the presence of fallback or recovery mechanisms. For example, a practitioner reported that “a guardrail exception fails to remove the prior agent response from the session history” (openai-agents-python #1840).

Interpretation: The Error Handling Issue category highlights challenges in LLM-based MAS related to runtime exception handling and system recovery mechanisms. The issues include Unhandled Exception (5) and Recovery Failure (7). Overall, these findings indicate that Error Handling Issues arise from the inability of systems to properly manage runtime errors and recover from execution breakdowns, leading to reduced reliability and interrupted multi-agent workflows.

3.1.16 Task Management Issue

(1.2%) Task Management Issue refers to issues arising from task assignment, scheduling, and task execution flow in LLM-based MAS. This category encompasses the following two types.

  • •

    Task Allocation Failure refers to issues where tasks are not handled by the appropriate agents in a multi-agent workflow, leading to incomplete task execution. For example, a practitioner reported that “a ‘RetrieveUserProxyAgent’ agent is sometimes not called when expected, preventing the intended retrieval task from being performed.” (AutoGen #1130).

  • •

    Task Duplication refers to issues where the same task is executed multiple times in a single run, leading to repeated agent executions and duplicated outputs. For example, a practitioner reported that agents are re-invoked after completing their first cycle, causing the pipeline to run again: “Agents work twice in every run” (CrewAI #416).

Interpretation: The Task Management Issue category highlights challenges in LLM-based MAS related to task allocation and execution control during multi-agent workflows. The issues include Task Allocation Failure (7) and Task Duplication (4). Overall, these findings indicate that incorrect task distribution and repeated task execution across agents can reduce coordination effectiveness and lead to inconsistencies in multi-agent workflow execution.

3.1.17 Security Issue

(0.3%) Security Issue refers to issues related to access control, data protection, and security vulnerabilities in LLM-based MAS. This category encompasses the following two types.

  • •

    Validation Issue refers to security issues where insufficient verification of input data leads to unsafe processing, resulting in security vulnerabilities or unintended system behavior. For example, a practitioner reported that pickle.loads is used without sufficient input validation, allowing unsafe code execution: “incoming agent data is unsafely deserialized using pickle.loads, allowing attackers to execute commands remotely” (AgentScope #635).

  • •

    Access Control Issue refers to security issues where permission control, or identity-based access mechanisms, are not properly implemented, leading to unauthorized access to user-specific resources. For example, a practitioner reported that “wrong user IDs cause agents to return data belonging to other users, resulting in unauthorized access to user-specific resources” (Agno #2279).

Interpretation: The Security Issue category highlights challenges in LLM-based MAS related to input validation and access control in LLM-based MAS. The issues include Validation Issue (2) and Access Control Issue (1). Overall, these findings indicate that security-related issues mainly arise from insufficient input validation and weak enforcement of access restrictions, which may lead to unsafe processing and unauthorized access in MAS.

3.2 Category of Causes (RQ2)

To address RQ2, we investigate the underlying causes of the issues identified in the final dataset. We categorize the extracted causes into distinct categories to characterize the factors contributing to issues in open-source LLM-based MAS. As mentioned in Section 2.4.2, not all closed issues have an associated cause that can be identified. However, an issue may have one or more causes, and all causes identified by the practitioner or development team are recorded. As a result, we identified a total of 540 causes, which were extracted from 57.2% of the 944 issues and categorized into 14 categories as presented in Table 6.

3.2.1 Results

The results show that the most prominent cause is Workflow Problem (WP) (29.4%), followed by Tool Integration Problem (TIP) (11.7%), and Memory Problem (MP) (11.1%). Examples of each category of cause, along with their counts and proportions, are also provided in Table 6. It should be noted that certain categories of issues can potentially serve as causes of other issues. For example, problems in the Agent Lifecycle Problem (ALP) category can disrupt workflow execution, leading to problems in the Workflow Problem (WP) category. Such failures may also disrupt inter-agent coordination and message exchange during execution, resulting in problems in the Communication Problem (CP) category.

  • •

    Workflow Problem (WP) refers to problems in workflow execution and task coordination in LLM-based MAS. These problems are caused by limitations in workflow design and execution, leading to incorrect, incomplete, or failed outcomes. It encompasses eleven types: (1) Context Management Problem: Problems arising from failures in transferring task-related context (e.g., instructions, communication history, or execution state) between agents during workflow execution, causing incorrect coordination or task outcomes. (2) Coordination Problem: Problems arising from weak interaction and synchronization among multiple agents. (3) Error Transmission Problem: Problems arising when failures in an earlier workflow step affect subsequent execution stages, causing incorrect task outcomes.

    (4) Handoff Data Problem: Problems arising when task-related data, execution context, or required parameters are missing or incompletely transferred during a handoff between agents. For example, a user reported that “required execution events were incorrectly classified and filtered out during the handoff” (Adk-Python #2073). (5) Loop Problem: Problems arising from missing or incorrect termination conditions or flawed control logic. (6) Message Routing Problem: Problems arising due to failures in processing, forwarding, or delivering messages between agents during execution.

    (7) Orchestration Problem: Problems arising from improper management of task dependencies and workflow execution across multiple agents, affecting overall execution flow. (8) Resource Contention Problem: Problems arising when multiple agents compete for limited shared resources (e.g., memory, files, tools, or execution slots) during concurrent execution, causing blocking, conflicts, or delayed task completion. (9) Sequential Execution Problem: Problems arising due to incorrect ordering or dependency conflicts in stepwise execution. (10) Workflow State Error: Problems arising from incorrect or inconsistent system state during a single workflow run, causing agents to act on outdated or corrupted intermediate data across sequential steps. (11) External Tool Problem: Problems arising when an external tool itself fails or produces unexpected outputs during workflow execution, despite being correctly integrated and invoked, resulting in incorrect or incomplete workflow outcomes.

  • •

    Tool Integration Problem (TIP) refers to problems concerning the integration and interaction of external tools in LLM-based MAS. These problems are caused by failures in integrating, invoking, or communicating with tools, including parameter handling, tool access, or schema consistency, leading to invocation failures, incorrect data transmission, or incomplete task outcomes. It encompasses four types: (1) MCP Integration Problem: Problems arising due to failures in integrating or communicating with external Model Context Protocol (MCP)-based systems. (2) Parameter Integration Problem: Problems arising due to required input parameters not being correctly passed to tools during invocation. (3) Tool Execution Problem: Problems arising due to failures in accessing or executing tools, where the tool cannot run as intended (e.g., resource locks, runtime crashes, timeouts). For example, a user explained that “Claude Code tools were already active or locked in the current session, preventing Claude-Flow from accessing them” (Claude-Flow #59). (4) Tool Schema Problem: Problems arising due to mismatches or inconsistencies between tool definitions and expected input or output schemas.

  • •

    Memory Problem (MP) refers to problems concerning the storage, retrieval, and utilization of memory in LLM-based MAS. These problems arise due to limitations in memory mechanisms or contextual consistency, leading to consistency errors and incorrect responses across sessions. It encompasses three types: (1) Memory Persistence Problem: Problems arising from failures in storing, retrieving, or retaining contextual information across execution steps, causing agents to lose previously established knowledge or states. (2) Memory Management Problem: Problems arising due to failures in storing or updating internal or external memory, affecting memory consistency and correctness. For example, a user explained that “external memory storage failed because agent roles were appended to the collection name, exceeding the allowed length” (CrewAI #2985). (3) State Management Problem: Problems arising due to inconsistent or incorrect maintenance of system state across interactions or sessions.

  • •

    Integration Problem (IP) refers to problems concerning the integration and compatibility of components in LLM-based MAS. These problems arise due to failures in component compatibility, coordination among agents, or configuration alignment across agents, models, and execution frameworks, leading to communication inconsistencies, configuration mismatches, and incorrect system behavior across workflows.
