It encompasses two types: (1) Agent Integration Problem: Problems arising due to failures in integrating agents within hierarchical MAS. For example, a user reported that “the issue occurred because the speaker-selection agent was not properly integrated with the custom model client” (AutoGen #2956). (2) Parameter Propagation Problem: Problems arising when required parameters or execution settings are not correctly transferred between interacting components in LLM-based MAS.

  • •

    Agent Lifecycle Problem (ALP) refers to problems concerning the lifecycle of agents in LLM-based MAS, including their creation, initialization, and execution. These problems arise from failures in agent initialization or runtime execution, leading to improper agent setup, execution failures, or inconsistent agent behavior. It encompasses two types: (1) Agent Creation Problem: Problems arising due to created agents not being properly initialized with required configurations or model clients. For example, a user reported that “a custom model client failed in a group chat because the internal speaker-selection agent was initialized without registering the custom model client” (AutoGen #2643). (2) Agent Runtime Problem: Problems arising when an agent fails to execute an assigned task correctly due to runtime errors or execution interruptions.

  • •

    Communication Problem (CP) refers to problems concerning the exchange of information between agents in LLM-based MAS. These problems arise due to failures in message passing, routing, or maintaining shared context among agents, leading to incorrect information transfer and disrupted execution continuity across the workflow. It encompasses three types: (1) Handoff Problem: Problems arising during the transfer of control, responsibility, or task ownership between agents, where the receiving agent fails to correctly continue execution. For example, a user reported that “a handoff between agents returned no task because the user message was added to the chat history after the LLM processed the handoff tool, making the message unavailable to the receiving agent” (PraisonAI #795). (2) Inter-Agent Communication Problem: Problems arising due to failures in delivering or routing messages between agents in LLM-based MAS. (3) Message Handling Problem: Problems arising due to incorrect processing, interpretation, or filtering of received messages within agents.

  • •

    Configuration Problem (ConP) refers to problems related to the setup and specification of parameters and system configurations in LLM-based MAS. These problems arise due to missing or incorrect configuration of models, agents, or execution frameworks, leading to initialization failures and runtime errors. It encompasses the following two types: (1) Setup Problem: Problems arising due to missing, incompatible, or incorrectly initialized configuration files or environment dependencies during MAS or agent setup. (2) Parameter Problem: Problems arising due to required parameters, model settings, or execution arguments being incorrectly specified or propagated. For example, a user reported that “CaptainAgent failed because the internal AgentBuilder ignored the explicitly provided LLMConfig parameter and instead looked for a legacy OAI_CONFIG_LIST file, causing a file-not-found error” (Ag2 #1446).

  • •

    Dependency Problem (DP) refers to problems concerning incompatibilities among system dependencies in LLM-based MAS. These problems arise due to mismatched, missing, or incompatible external APIs or modules, leading to execution failures or runtime errors. It encompasses three types: (1) API Compatibility Problem: Problems arising due to incompatible or changed API interfaces. (2) Import Problem: Problems arising due to missing or improperly loaded modules, files, or configuration imports. (3) Version Compatibility Problem: Problems arising due to mismatched or incompatible software versions following upgrades or changes in the execution environment. For example, a user reported that “upgrading Flowise to v3.0.3 caused existing AgentFlow v1 flows to fail due to incompatibility between the updated dependencies and the existing flow configuration” (Flowise #4756).

  • •

    Documentation Problem (DocP) refers to problems concerning incomplete or inconsistent documentation in LLM-based MAS. These problems arise due to missing, outdated, or inconsistent documentation, leading to usability issues, configuration errors, or incorrect system execution. It encompasses two types: (1) Missing Documentation: Problems arising due to required information not being provided in documentation. (2) Outdated Documentation: Problems arising due to documentation not being updated after system changes. For example, a user reported that a “sub-agent execution failed because the documentation incorrectly instructed hooks notification while the actual command expected hooks notify” (Claude-flow #504).

  • •

    Performance Problem (PP) refers to problems concerning the efficiency and speed of LLM-based MAS. These problems arise due to limitations in parallel execution, scalability, timeouts, or processing latency, leading to slow execution or high resource usage. It encompasses four types: (1) Parallel Execution Problem: Problems arising due to failures in concurrent execution across agents. (2) Scalability Problem: Problems arising due to reduced performance as system size or workload increases.(3) Timeout Problem: Problems arising when operations exceed the allowed execution time. (4) Latency Problem: Problems arising due to delays caused by inefficient processing or large data operations. For example, a user explained that “shared memory access became slow as the dataset grew because load() used deepcopy() on every call, and duplicate records led to increased memory usage, resulting in high latency” (Camel #3185).

  • •

    Database Problem (DataP) refers to problems concerning database structure, initialization, data access, and schema consistency in LLM-based MAS. These problems arise due to failures in database setup, data retrieval, or schema alignment, leading to execution failures or incorrect system behavior. It encompasses three types: (1) Database Initialization Failure: Problems arising due to errors during database creation or setup. (2) Data Retrieval Failure: Problems arising due to failure in accessing or retrieving required data. (3) Database Schema Inconsistency: Problems arising due to mismatches between expected and actual database schema. For example, a user reported that “agent creation failed because the agents table lacked the role column that the application expected during data insertion” (Claude-Flow #403).

  • •

    Infrastructure Problem (InfP) refers to problems concerning the technical infrastructure, execution environment, and deployment of LLM-based MAS. These problems arise due to failures or limitations in system infrastructure, deployment environments, or file handling, leading to execution failures or system unavailability. It encompasses three types: (1) Server Problem: Problems arising from server configuration, availability, or resource limitations. (2) File System Handling Problem: Problems arising from file access, storage, or path-related issues. (3) Deployment Problem: Problems arising from infrastructure or runtime environment issues during system deployment. For example, a user explained that “AI agents failed to be created in a Kubernetes deployment because network policies prevented pods from reaching external URLs, causing connection timeouts to external AI providers” (Activepieces #9038).

  • •

    Frontend Problem (FP) refers to problems concerning the user interface and output handling of LLM-based MAS. These problems arise due to failures or limitations in user interface rendering, event propagation, or output display, leading to incorrect, incomplete, or unavailable information being presented to users. It encompasses two types: (1) User Interface Problem: Problems arising from failures in rendering or presenting the user interface during MAS execution. (2) Output Problem: Problems arising from failures or limitations in displaying, updating, or streaming agent outputs. For example, a user explained that “streaming agent outputs are truncated when fixed-position boxes run out of available display space, preventing the display from scrolling to the latest output” (Agno #3680).

  • •

    Security Problem (SP) refers to problems concerning vulnerabilities that expose LLM-based MAS to unauthorized access, malicious execution, or unauthorized manipulation of system control. These problems arise due to weaknesses in input validation, deserialization, or function access control, leading to system compromise or unauthorized actions. It encompasses two types: (1) Prompt Injection Problem: Problems arising due to manipulation of model inputs to alter system behavior or bypass constraints. (2) Insecure Deserialization Problem: Problems arising due to unsafe deserialization of malicious data, potentially allowing unauthorized code execution. For example, a user explained that “the system unsafely deserialized incoming agent data using a vulnerable deserialization method, allowing malicious code execution” (Agentscope #635).

3.2.2 Causes to Issues Mapping

Table 7 illustrates the mapping between Issue categories and Cause categories identified in the development and use of open-source LLM-based MAS, along with their distributions. To improve readability, abbreviations are used to denote each Cause category for instance, “WP” refers to Workflow Problem. The full names of all Cause categories are provided in the note of Table 7.

Over three quarters, 87.0% of Implementation Issue are associated with identified causes, representing the highest rate among all issue categories. These issues are mainly caused by Workflow Problem (WP) (24).

Only 13.6% of Feature Request cases are associated with identified causes, representing the lowest rate among all issue categories. Workflow Problem (WP) (7) is identified as the most frequent cause.

The largest category among all issues is Orchestration & Execution Issue. 54.8% of these issues are associated with identified causes, and the most frequent causes are Workflow Problem (WP) (65), Agent Lifecycle Problem (ALP) (10), and Integration Problem (IP) (9).

For Error Handling Issue, causes are identified in 83.3% of cases. These issues mainly originate from Tool Integration Problem (TIP) (3).

For Tool Issue, 73.6% of cases are associated with identified causes. These issues mainly originate from Tool Integration Problem (TIP) (23) and Workflow Problem (WP) (18).

For Integration Issue, causes are identified in 71.4% of cases, mainly arising from Integration Problem (IP) (17).

For Environment & Configuration Issue, causes are identified in 69.7% of cases, mainly arising from Dependency Problem (DP) (7) and Configuration Problem (ConP) (7).

For Compatibility Issue, causes are identified in 69.2% of cases, mainly arising from Communication Problem (CP) (3).

For Model Issue, causes are identified in 66.7% of cases, mainly originating from Workflow Problem (WP) (4).

For Security Issue, causes are identified in 66.7% of cases, mainly originating from Security Problem (SP) (2).

For Memory & State Management Issue, causes are identified in 60.4% of cases. These issues mainly originate from Memory Problem (MP) (43).

For Communication Issue, causes are identified in 64.0% of cases. These issues mainly originate from Communication Problem (CP) (11).

For Role Issue, causes are identified in 52.8% of cases. These issues are mainly caused by Workflow Problem (WP) (7).

For Documentation Issue, causes are identified in 57.7% of cases. These issues mainly originate from Documentation Problem (DocP) (10).

For Output Issue, causes are identified in 48.3% of cases. These issues are mainly caused by Integration Problem (IP) (3), Workflow Problem (WP) (3), and Frontend Problem (FP) (3).

For Performance Issue, causes are identified in 36.8% of cases. These issues are mainly caused by Memory Problem (MP) (2), Workflow Problem (WP) (2), and Performance Problem (PP) (2).

For Task Management Issue, causes are identified in 36.4% of cases. These issues are mainly caused by Workflow Problem (WP) (4).

3.2.3 Interpretation

In this section, we analyze the frequency and distribution of different causes across various issue categories in LLM-based MAS. We further map these causes to specific issue types to identify the dominant root causes associated with different issues.

Frequency of the causes: The frequency of the causes shows that Workflow Problem (WP) is the most frequent cause of issues, as the results indicate. Since LLM-based MAS rely on sequential execution and shared context, most failures arise from incorrect workflow state handling and repeated use of outdated context, leading to incorrect outputs. This highlights workflow consistency as a key challenge in multi-agent coordination. Tool Integration Problem (TIP) and Memory Problem (MP) also significantly contribute to issues in LLM-based MAS. TIP reflects failures in tool registration or invocation, where agents cannot access required external tools. Memory Problem (MP) indicates failures in retaining or retrieving contextual information across agent interactions, causing agents in LLM-based MAS to lose previously established context during task execution. Together, Tool Integration Problem (TIP) and Memory Problem (MP) represent important causes of issues in LLM-based MAS, particularly those related to tool integration and memory management. Additionally, Integration Problem (IP), Agent Lifecycle Problem (ALP), Communication Problem (CP), and Configuration Problem (ConP) appear with moderate frequency. These causes mainly concern system setup and coordination, including incorrect configurations, naming constraints, and message misinterpretation. Although less frequent than WP, these causes reflect important challenges in configuring and coordinating LLM-based MAS. The remaining categories, including Dependency Problem (DP), Documentation Problem (DocP), Performance Problem (PP), Database Problem (DataP), Infrastructure Problem (InfP), Frontend Problem (FP) and Security Problem (SP), occur less frequently but still impact system stability, usability, scalability, and security of LLM-based MAS. Overall, most causes are concentrated in workflow execution, tool usage, and memory handling, while the remaining categories represent other underlying causes in LLM-based MAS.

Mapping of causes to issues: Workflow Problem (WP) is the most frequent cause across multiple issue categories. 57.0% of Orchestration & Execution Issue causes originate from Workflow Problem (WP), reflecting the central role of workflow design in agent coordination and task execution. Similarly, 51.2% of Memory & State Management Issue cases are caused by Memory Problem (MP), highlighting the close relationship between workflow execution and memory handling when agents lose context or state updates are not properly propagated. Tool Integration Problem (TIP) is the dominant cause of Tool Issue, accounting for 35.9% of cases. These issues typically arise from tool execution failures, invocation errors, and schema mismatches. Integration Problem (IP) is the primary cause of Integration Issue, accounting for 37.7% of cases, reflecting the challenges of coordinating multiple components, APIs, and frameworks within the MAS. Overall, Workflow Problem (WP) and Tool Integration Problem (TIP) are the most dominant root causes of issues in LLM-based MAS. This highlights the importance of robust workflow design and reliable tool integration in LLM-based MAS.

3.3 Category of Solutions (RQ3)

To address RQ3, we investigate the solutions used to resolve the identified issues in open-source LLM-based MAS. We categorize the identified solutions into distinct categories to characterize the approaches practitioners use to address the issues. As mentioned in Section 2.4.2, not all closed issues have an associated solution that can be identified. As a result, we identified a total of 427 solutions, which were used to address 45.2% of the 944 issues, and categorized them into 10 categories as presented in Table 8.

3.3.1 Results

The results show that Optimize Workflow (OW) is the most commonly utilized solution, accounting for 26.0% of the total solutions, followed by Adjust Configuration (AC), Optimize Tool Integration (OTI), and Optimize Infrastructure (OI), accounting for 15.0%, 11.9%, and 11.0%, respectively.

  • •

    Optimize Workflow (OW) refers to improving workflow execution and task coordination in LLM-based MAS. It can be categorized into five types: (1) Enhance Orchestration: refers to adjusting strategies for coordination and task allocation among agents. (2) Enhance State Management: refers to adjusting strategies for managing execution states and intermediate data across agents. (3) Fix Loop Issues: refers to resolving infinite or unnecessary execution loops in workflow execution. (4) Implement Parallel Execution: refers to adjusting execution strategies to enable concurrent task processing across agents. (5) Optimize Sequential Execution: refers to optimizing execution strategies to ensure efficient workflow progression and data exchange between agents. For example, a user proposed “adding an agent parameter to tool hooks and injecting data keys into the LLM context to reduce token usage and latency when transferring large datasets between agents” (Agno #3712).

  • •

    Adjust Configuration (AC) refers to modifying system settings and parameters in LLM-based MAS. It can be categorized into four types: (1) Refine Prompt: refers to adjusting prompt design to guide agent behavior. (2) Modify Runtime Parameter: refers to adjusting execution parameters to control runtime behavior. For example, a user proposed “adding a runtime parameter to execute only the latest message, preventing unintended code execution in multi-agent chats” (Autogen #5283). (3) Configure External Dependency: refers to configuring external tools or libraries required for agents to perform tasks within LLM-based MAS. (4) Update Environment Configuration: refers to adjusting environment-level settings required for the compatibility and correct execution of LLM-based MAS.

  • •

    Optimize Tool Integration (OTI) refers to improving tool connectivity and execution behavior in LLM-based MAS. It can be categorized into two types: (1) Fix Tool Execution: refers to resolving tool execution problems caused by execution flow issues or errors in LLM-based MAS. (2) Tool Integration Fix: refers to resolving issues in tool registration, connectivity, or compatibility within LLM-based MAS. For example, a user suggested that “connecting and closing MCP tools through the FastAPI application lifespan to resolve MCP connectivity failures” (Agno #4958).

  • •

    Optimize Infrastructure (OI) refers to improving infrastructure components and resource management in LLM-based MAS. It can be categorized into two types: (1) Database Compatibility: refers to resolving incompatibilities in database backends and storage systems due to improper configuration in LLM-based MAS. (2) Optimize Memory Management: refers to improving memory initialization, synchronization, and persistence to ensure reliable memory handling across agents in LLM-based MAS. For example, a user resolved “the unknown memory backend: undefined error by adding required configuration parameters and creating a default SQLite configuration with a 50MB cache and 30s synchronization interval” (Claude-flow #354).

  • •

    Improve Error Handling (IEH) refers to the process of solving problems by improving error detection, exception management, and recovery behavior in LLM-based MAS. It can be categorized into four types: (1) Fix Error Propagation: refers to addressing situations in which an error generated by one agent or workflow step is propagated to subsequent agents or steps without being properly communicated, detected, or handled, potentially causing downstream execution failures. (2) Enhance Fallback Mechanism: refers to improving fallback strategies to maintain workflow execution when agents or tools fail in LLM-based MAS. (3) Enhance Handoff Message Flow: refers to improving message routing and conversation continuity during agent handoffs in LLM-based MAS. (4) Enhance Exception Handling: refers to improving exception management through retry logic, clearer error reporting, and recovery mechanisms to handle failures during LLM-based MAS execution. For example, a user proposed enhancing exception handling by “adding retry logic, circuit breakers, health checks, and clearer API error messages to manage external service failures more effectively” (Claude-flow #183).

  • •

    Optimize Communication (OC) refers to improving information exchange between agents in LLM-based MAS. It can be categorized into two types: (1) Optimize Message Handling: refers to improving message processing, including parsing, formatting, and response transformation within agents or communication modules in LLM-based MAS. (2) Optimize Inter-Agent Communication: refers to improving the exchange of messages between agents to ensure correct delivery, interpretation, and coordination across agents. For example, a user suggested that “correcting the serialization of response data in the remote agent client can prevent agent-to-agent communication failures” (Adk-Python #2921).

  • •

    Update Dependencies (UD) refers to solving dependency-related problems, including missing, mismatched, or incompatible libraries and package versions in LLM-based MAS. It can be categorized into two types: (1) Add Missing Dependency: refers to installing required libraries that are missing from the environment for LLM-based MAS. (2) Fix Version Compatibility: refers to resolving dependency version errors by aligning dependent library and package versions to ensure correct integration in LLM-based MAS. For example, a user resolved “the issue by updating the outdated Pydantic dependency from version 2.5.2 to the latest version” (Agno #2444).

  • •

    Adjust Agent Initialization (AAI) refers to adjusting agent setup and initialization in LLM-based MAS. It can be categorized into three types: (1) Fix Import Path Resolution: refers to resolving issues where agent modules or definitions cannot be correctly located or loaded in LLM-based MAS. (2) Correct Agent Initialization: refers to improving dynamic agent creation and registration to ensure that required agent types are correctly initialized and available in LLM-based MAS. For example, a user resolved “the issue by replacing the incorrect knowledge_sources parameter with the expected knowledge parameter when creating agents” (PraisonAI #404). (3) Configure Agent Integration: refers to configuring the connections between agents and their required components, such as knowledge sources, models, or tools, during agent initialization in LLM-based MAS.

  • •

    Improve Documentation (ID) refers to improving the clarity and completeness of documentation in LLM-based MAS. It can be categorized into two types: (1) Modify Documentation: refers to modifying or updating existing documentation to better clarify system behavior or usage instructions in LLM-based MAS. (2) Add Documentation: refers to adding missing guidance, examples, or workflow descriptions for system features in LLM-based MAS. For example, a user provided “documentation and examples for AgentTool usage in multi-agent workflows” (Adk-Python #1608).

  • •

    Improve Frontend (IF) refers to improving the user interface and output presentation of LLM-based MAS. It can be categorized into two types: (1) Enhance UI Interaction: refers to improving how users interact with LLM-based MAS through interface controls, input mechanisms, and interactive features. (2) Enhance UI Display: refers to improving the presentation, updating, and streaming of agent outputs in LLM-based MAS. For example, a user proposed “displaying agent names in chat messages to clarify which agent is communicating” (AutoGen #5609).

3.3.2 Solutions to Issues Mapping

Table 9 illustrates the mapping of Issue categories to Solution categories, along with their distribution, using abbreviations to represent each category of solution. For example, “OTI” represents Optimize Tool Integration. The full names of all solution categories are provided in the note of Table 9.

For Documentation Issue, 76.9% of cases are well addressed, reaching the highest resolution rate among all issue categories. Improve Documentation (ID) (9) is identified as the most frequent solution for resolving Documentation Issue.

For Output Issue, 24.1% of cases are reported as resolved, reaching the lowest resolution rate among all issue categories, and Output Issue is mostly solved by Improve Error Handling (IEH) (2).

For Orchestration & Execution Issue, which is the largest issue category, 37.9% of cases have effective solutions. Orchestration & Execution Issue is mostly addressed by Optimize Workflow (OW) (38).

For Implementation Issue, 69.0% of cases are well addressed. The most frequently used solution for Implementation Issue is Optimize Workflow (OW) (18).

For Compatibility Issue, solutions are identified in 61.5% of cases. Update Dependencies (UD) (2) and Optimize Communication (OC) (2) are the most frequently employed solutions to resolve Compatibility Issue.

For Error Handling Issue, 66.7% of cases are well resolved. The most frequently employed solution for Error Handling Issue is Improve Error Handling (IEH) (5).

For Environment & Configuration Issue, 54.5% of cases have effective solutions. Update Dependencies (UD) (8) is identified as the most frequently used solution to address the Environment & Configuration Issue.

For Integration Issue, solutions are identified in 50.8% of cases. The most frequently employed solutions for Integration Issue are Adjust Configuration (AC) (7) and Optimize Tool Integration (OTI) (7).

For Role Issue, 47.2% of cases are effectively addressed. The most frequently employed solutions to address Role Issues are Adjust Agent Initialization (AAI) (5) and Adjust Configuration (AC) (5).

For Memory & State Management Issue, 43.2% of cases are addressed by practitioners. The most frequently employed solution for Memory & State Management Issue is Optimize Infrastructure (OI) (23).

For Tool Issue, solutions are identified in 45.9% of cases. Optimize Tool Integration (OTI) (12) is the most commonly applied solution to resolve Tool Issue.

For Model Issue, 40.0% of cases are resolved. The most frequently used solution to address Model Issue is Optimize Tool Integration (OTI) (2).

For Task Management Issue, 36.4% of cases are resolved by practitioners. Optimize Workflow (OW) (3) is identified as the most commonly applied solution to address Task Management Issue.

For Feature Request, 35.2% of cases are well addressed by practitioners. The most commonly employed solution for Feature Requests is Optimize Communication (OC) (12).

For Communication Issue, 36.0% of cases are well resolved by practitioners. Optimize Communication (OC) (4) is identified as the most frequently employed solution for Communication Issue.

For Security Issue, 33.3% of cases are resolved. The most frequently used solution to address Security Issue is Optimize Communication (OC) (1).

For Performance Issue, 26.3% of cases are well resolved by practitioners. Adjust Configuration (AC) (2) is identified as the most frequently employed solution for Performance Issue.

3.3.3 Interpretation

In this section, we analyze the frequency and distribution of different solutions across various issue categories in LLM-based MAS. We further map these solutions to specific issue types to identify the dominant solutions used to address different issues.

Frequency of the solutions: Optimize Workflow (OW), Adjust Configuration (AC), Optimize Tool Integration (OTI), and Optimize Infrastructure (OI) are the most frequently used solutions in LLM-based MAS due to their direct impact on execution flow, configuration, tool usage, and infrastructure reliability. Optimize Workflow (OW) is widely applied because MAS depend on proper orchestration, state sharing, and task coordination to ensure smooth execution. Adjust Configuration (AC) is also a common solution since incorrect prompts, runtime settings, or environment configurations often lead to system errors, making parameter adjustment a frequent fix strategy in LLM-based MAS. Optimize Tool Integration (OTI) is another major category of solutions, as LLM-based MAS rely heavily on external tools and APIs, where integration or execution issues can easily break workflows between agents. Optimize Communication (OC) is a similarly important solution category because reliable inter-agent communication is essential for correct message exchange and task completion in LLM-based MAS. Although Update Dependencies (UD), Adjust Agent Initialization (AAI), Improve Error Handling (IEH), Improve Documentation (ID), and Improve Frontend (IF) are employed less frequently, they remain important for MAS stability. For example, Optimize Infrastructure (OI) shows that practitioners resolve system failures by improving memory and database infrastructure to ensure stable execution and data persistence in LLM-based MAS.

Mapping of solutions to issues: Optimize Workflow (OW) is the most dominant solution category, accounting for 26.0% of all identified solutions. For Orchestration & Execution Issue, which is the largest issue category, Optimize Workflow (OW) addresses 48.1% of cases, reflecting the critical role of workflow optimization in resolving agent coordination and execution failures. Similarly, Adjust Configuration (AC) is the second most common solution (15.0%), and it accounts for 21.9% of solutions for Integration Issue. Optimize Tool Integration (OTI) accounts for 11.9% of solutions and is the most frequent solution for Tool Issues, accounting for 30.0% of cases, reflecting the reliance of MAS on external tools and the need for robust tool integration mechanisms. Optimize Infrastructure (OI) is the fourth most common solution, accounting for 11.0% of all identified solutions, and is predominantly applied to address Memory & State Management Issues. Documentation Issue has the highest resolution rate of 76.0%, while Output Issue has the lowest resolution rate 24.1%. Overall, the predominance of Optimize Workflow (OW), Adjust Configuration (AC), Optimize Tool Integration (OTI), and Optimize Infrastructure (OI) across multiple issue categories indicates that practitioners primarily focus on workflow execution, configuration management, and tool integration when resolving issues in LLM-based MAS.

4 Implications

In this section, we discuss the implications of the study results presented in Section 3 for users, developers, and researchers of open-source LLM-based MAS.

4.1 Implications for Users of LLM-based MAS

Orchestration & Execution Issue (22.0%) ranks first among all 17 issue categories, and within this category, Coordination & Handoff Issue is the dominant type, indicating that users frequently face difficulties in coordinating task transfers and managing execution flow in LLM-based MAS. A practitioner reported that “the sub-agent could not correctly transfer control back to the root agent when calling an MCP tool” (Adk-python #1039), suggesting that unclear handoff specifications can lead to agents coordination failures. Several practices can improve coordination among agents and enhance the reliability of task execution in LLM-based MAS. For example, users can define explicit handoff prompts or utilize built-in agent handoff mechanisms provided by frameworks such as OpenAI Agents SDK (OpenAI, 2025b) to clearly specify transfer conditions and task responsibilities between agents. Furthermore, users can configure framework-level execution controls, such as retry limits, timeout settings, and logging mechanisms, to reduce infinite loops, premature termination, and unexpected execution behaviors in LLM-based MAS. In addition, many LLM-based multi-agent frameworks provide orchestration and monitoring capabilities that support workflow design, inspection, and debugging, enabling early detection of coordination issues and improving collaboration reliability between agents (Dibia et al., 2024). For example, citecemri2025multi conducted a comprehensive empirical study on multi-agent failure modes and found that inter-agent misalignment, including communication breakdowns, context loss during handoffs, and conflicting outputs, accounts for 36.9% of failures across seven MAS frameworks. Consequently, users should prioritize explicit handoff design and systematic execution monitoring to address Orchestration & Execution Issue, the most common issue category in LLM-based MAS.

One-third of the open-source LLM-based MAS investigated in this study are frameworks for developing software applications by leveraging multiple collaborating LLM agents (see Table 3). These frameworks lower the barrier for users to build applications using LLM-based MAS. For example, AutoGen is an open-source framework that enables users to build LLM applications using multiple agents that can communicate with each other to accomplish tasks (Wu et al., 2024). It also allows users to configure agents with different commercial and open-source LLMs, according to their application requirements, enabling users to select a model that best fits their needs. While such frameworks provide useful capabilities for software development, our findings show that LLM-based MAS also face several problems. Specifically, Orchestration & Execution Issue, Memory & State Management Issue, Tool Issue, and Integration Issue account for 22.0%, 14.7%, 9.2%, and 6.7% of the issues, respectively. These findings suggest that using open-source LLM-based MAS for software development may introduce various challenges. Users should therefore monitor agent workflows, manage agent memory and state, verify tool usage, and configure explicit agent communication mechanisms when deploying and using LLM-based MAS.

4.2 Implications for Developers of LLM-based MAS

According to our study results, the following knowledge is required to develop and use open-source LLM-based MAS: (1) Developers need knowledge of designing and managing agent workflows and orchestration in LLM-based MAS. Our findings show that Workflow Problem (WP) accounts for 29.4% and ranks first among all identified causes. This indicates that developers need solid knowledge of agent coordination, handoff design, and execution flow management when developing LLM-based MAS. For example, a contributor reported that “after invoking transfer_to_agent, the target agent did not respond and produced no output due to incomplete transfer of task-related information” (Adk-python #2073), highlighting the importance of proper handoff design while developing LLM-based MAS. (2) Developers need to understand tool integration and execution in LLM-based MAS. According to our study results, Tool Integration Problem (TIP) accounts for 11.7% of all causes. This indicates that developers require knowledge of tool registration, schema validation, and concurrent tool access management when developing LLM-based MAS. For example, a developer reported that a “tool deadlock occurred because the swarm could not access tools already locked by an active Claude Code session” (Claude-flow #59), highlighting that knowledge of proper tool lifecycle management is essential when developing LLM-based MAS. (3) Developers need to understand memory management and state persistence in LLM-based MAS. Memory Problem (MP) accounts for 11.1% of all causes. For example, a developer explained that “external memory failed to store new memories in Mem0 because the agent ID exceeded the allowed length” (CrewAI #2985), indicating that knowledge of session persistence and state consistency is essential for developing reliable LLM-based MAS.

Tool Integration Problem (TIP) accounts for 11.7% of all identified causes, with Tool Execution Problem and MCP Integration Problem being the most frequently observed types. A typical failure occurs when tools encounter deadlocks, resource contention, or schema mismatches at runtime in LLM-based MAS. For example, a practitioner reported that “MCP tool calls failed during asynchronous GroupChat execution because the event loop was already running” (Ag2 #1763), while another reported that “VertexAI Search Tool failed when combined with a sub-agent because multiple tool types were not supported together” (Adk-Python #2822). To avoid such failures, developers should provide standardized tool validation APIs that automatically check input/output schemas when tools are configured, enforce timeouts at the tool level, and check tool availability before execution in LLM-based MAS. Additionally, since concurrent tool access by multiple agents can cause session locks, connection failures, and timeouts, MAS frameworks should provide mechanisms for managing tool connections, handling tool connection failures, and retrying failed tool calls. One practitioner reported that “managing tool connections through framework-provided lifecycle hooks (e.g., FastAPI lifespan in Agno) prevented MCP connection failures” (Agno #4958), highlighting the importance of proper tool lifecycle management for reliable MCP integration in LLM-based MAS.

4.3 Implications for Researchers of LLM-based MAS

Orchestration & Execution Issue, accounting for 22.0% of all reported issues, represents the most critical challenge in LLM-based MAS. Within this category, Coordination & Handoff Issue and Control Flow Error are the most frequent types, highlighting that failures often originate from coordination deficiencies and execution management challenges among agents. This finding is further supported by the root cause analysis, which identifies Workflow Problem (WP) as the most significant underlying factor, accounting for 29.4% of all reported causes. Moreover, Workflow Problem (WP) accounts for 57.0% of the causes associated with Orchestration & Execution Issue. This indicates that deficiencies in multi-agent workflow design, execution flow among agents, and inter-agent task coordination are major factors contributing to system-level failures in LLM-based MAS. We encourage researchers to shift their focus from enhancing individual agents reasoning capabilities toward developing robust orchestration frameworks that ensure reliable handoffs between agents, correct execution order across the agents, and appropriate termination conditions in LLM-based MAS. Specifically, future work could investigate the formal verification of agent workflows and the development of runtime monitoring mechanisms capable of detecting and correcting coordination anomalies, such as infinite loops and premature termination, before they propagate throughout the system.

Given the complex and dynamic behavior of LLM-based MAS, 27 of the 128 unsolved issues involve difficulties in reproducing the reported problems. Without accurately reproducing the problem within LLM-based MAS, it can be difficult for practitioners to identify root causes of the issues, thereby hindering the resolution of the issues. For example, practitioners reported that the “transfer_task_to_member error occasionally occurs in some random cases when using the aprint_response method” (Agno #3095), with multiple users experiencing different behaviors across versions. Identifying the root cause, in this case, a shared model instance issue, requires substantial investigation, highlighting the challenges of reproducing issues in LLM-based MAS and complicating their resolution. Therefore, future research could explore automated failure-reproduction techniques, controlled execution environments, and systematic test-case generation to improve the reproducibility of failures in LLM-based MAS.

Memory & State Management Issue represents the second most frequent challenge in LLM-based MAS, accounting for 14.7% of all reported issues. Within this category, Context Loss and State Inconsistency are the most common types, indicating limitations in current memory mechanisms in LLM-based MAS. This finding is further supported by the root cause analysis, which identifies Memory Problem (MP) as the third most significant underlying cause among all identified causes, accounting for 11.1% of all reported causes. Memory & State Management Issue accounts for 51.1% of the issues caused by Memory Problem (MP). This indicates that deficiencies in context propagation between agents, state synchronization across agents, and memory retrieval for agent interactions are major contributors to system failures in LLM-based MAS. We recommend that future research focus on developing reliable memory management mechanisms that ensure (1) consistent context propagation across agents during handoffs, (2) reliable state synchronization during parallel agent execution, and (3) effective context compression to prevent context overflow while preserving information essential for agent reasoning.

5 Threats to Validity

Construct validity: In our study, data collection was conducted automatically using GitHub APIs, while data filtering and labeling involved both automated and manual processes. Since several phases, including manual filtering, open coding, constant comparison, and data extraction, were performed manually, the study may be subject to personal bias during the classification, labeling, and extraction of issues, causes, and solutions in LLM-based MAS. To reduce this risk and improve the objectivity and reliability of the results, pilot studies were conducted using both automated and manual approaches before each formal phase to evaluate the effectiveness of methods, prompts, and criteria across different researchers, thereby improving construct validity. Following each pilot and formal study, we first performed automated filtering to obtain initial results. The first author then conducted a manual analysis and discussed the findings with the second and third authors to reach a consensus on the results related to the RQs. Since open coding and constant comparison were mainly carried out by the first author, there is still a risk of subjective interpretation affecting the results. The first author’s six years of software development experience, along with two years of experience working with LLM-based MASs, helped mitigate this risk, although it could not be eliminated entirely. In addition, future work may adopt more advanced automated or semi-automated techniques to further reduce bias in data filtering, labeling, and extraction.

External validity: In our study, the main threat to external validity comes from the selection of data sources. To address this, we used the “Issues” pages of GitHub projects as the primary data source. GitHub is the largest platform for hosting open-source projects. Each project includes an “Issues” section. Practitioners use it to report bugs, errors, and development difficulties. It also allows discussion between users and developers. To extract more reliable information on causes and solutions, we focused on closed issues. These usually contain resolved discussions and more complete resolution details of issues. However, even with these selection choices, we acknowledge that the dataset may not fully represent all practices in the development and use of LLM-based MAS. Some relevant information may reside outside GitHub or in undocumented settings, which could be explored as potential sources in future work.

Reliability: To address potential uncertainties arising from the research methodology, we took several steps to improve the reliability of this study. As described in Section 2.3.1, we first conducted pilot studies to check the agreement between the first and third authors on data labeling before starting the formal study. In this pilot phase, Cohen’s Kappa value was 0.82, which indicated a good level of agreement. During the data labeling, extraction, and analysis stages, we regularly discussed cases where there were differences in interpretation. These discussions helped us resolve disagreements and keep the results consistent across different stages of the study. This also improved the overall stability of the findings. In addition, the dataset used in this study has been made publicly available (Rehman et al., 2026), so that other researchers can replicate the study and validate the results independently.

6 Related Work

The existing literature is organized into three categories. We first review empirical studies using software repository mining to investigate practitioner-reported issues, causes, and solutions in software systems and LLM-based projects in Section 6.1. We then discuss LLM-based MAS for software engineering in Section 6.2, followed by studies exploring challenges, failure patterns, and limitations of LLM-based MAS in Section 6.3. Finally, we summarize the research gaps motivating this study in Section 6.4.

6.1 Mining Software Repositories for Exploring Issues, Causes, and Solutions

Mining software repositories has become a widely used approach for understanding practitioner-reported issues, their underlying causes, and corresponding solutions. Waseem et al. (2021) conducted an empirical study to understand issues in open-source microservice systems. They manually analyzed 1,345 closed GitHub issues from five projects and developed a taxonomy of 17 issue categories. Their results show that Technical Debt, Build, and Security are the most frequently reported categories. They later extended this work by analyzing 2,641 GitHub issues from 15 open-source microservice systems. They also conducted 15 practitioner interviews and surveyed 150 practitioners. Based on these findings, they developed comprehensive taxonomies of issues, root causes, and solutions in microservice systems. Zhao et al. (2023b) conducted a large-scale empirical study of 570 performance issues from 13 open-source projects. They identified eight common root causes and corresponding solutions. Their findings show that 27% of the issues require design-level optimization, highlighting the importance of architectural improvements for addressing performance issues. With the growing adoption of AI and LLMs in software engineering, researchers have extended repository mining to investigate practitioner-reported issues in LLM-based projects. Cai et al. (2025b) analyzed 994 GitHub issues from 15 open-source LLM projects. They developed taxonomies of issue categories, root causes, and solutions. Their results show that Model Issue is the most common issue category, while Model Problem, Configuration Problem, and Connection Problem are the most frequent root causes. Model Optimization is the predominant solution. Zhou et al. (2025b) investigated GitHub Copilot, an LLM-based AI programming assistant, by analyzing 473 GitHub issues, 706 GitHub discussions, and 142 Stack Overflow posts. Their findings show that Operation Issue and Compatibility Issue are the most common problem categories. Copilot Internal Error, Network Connection Error, and IDE Compatibility Issue are the most frequent causes, while Bug Fixed by Copilot, Modify Configuration, and Use Suitable Version are the predominant solutions. Collectively, these studies establish a foundation for understanding practitioner-reported issues, their root causes, and solutions through repository mining across different software domains.

6.2 LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems for Software Engineering

Recent advances in LLMs have led to the emergence of LLM-based MAS, where multiple specialized agents collaborate to automate software engineering tasks. Qian et al. (2024) introduced ChatDev, a chat-powered software development framework that assigns specialized roles (e.g., CEO, CTO, Programmer, Reviewer, and Tester) to LLM-based agents. By using a chat chain to decompose tasks and support sequential interactions among agents, ChatDev enables collaborative software development and achieves an 88% executability score, reflecting the proportion of software projects generated by ChatDev that successfully compile and execute. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of LLM-based MAS for software development. Likewise, Hong et al. (2024) introduced MetaGPT, a meta-programming framework that incorporates Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) into multi-agent collaboration. By assigning specialized roles to agents and enforcing structured workflows, MetaGPT enables agents to collaboratively perform software engineering tasks through role-based coordination. Similarly, Wu et al. (2024) introduced AutoGen, a generalized multi-agent conversation framework for developing LLM-based applications. AutoGen enables agents to perform tasks using LLMs, human feedback, and external tools, while supporting flexible communication patterns for designing complex multi-agent workflows. AutoGen achieves 69.48% accuracy on the MATH dataset, a standard benchmark comprising 12,500 high-school competition math problems, substantially outperforming vanilla GPT-4. In addition, Nguyen et al. (2025) introduced AgileCoder, a multi-agent software development framework inspired by Agile methodology. AgileCoder assigns specialized roles (e.g., Product Manager, Scrum Master, Developer, and Tester) to agents and organizes development into iterative sprints based on user feedback. It further introduces a Dynamic Code Graph Generator to maintain code dependencies and provide relevant context for code generation and modification. Evaluations on HumanEval, MBPP, and ProjectDev show that AgileCoder outperforms existing frameworks such as ChatDev and MetaGPT, demonstrating the effectiveness of integrating Agile principles into multi-agent software development. To provide a broader perspective on designing LLM-based MAS for software engineering tasks, Cai et al. (2025a) examined the quality attributes, design patterns, and design rationale adopted in existing LLM-based MAS. Their analysis shows that Code Generation is the most frequently addressed software engineering task, Functional Suitability is the most emphasized quality attribute, and Role-Based Cooperation and Self-Reflection are the most commonly adopted design patterns. They also report that improving code quality and simulating human problem-solving are the primary motivations behind these design choices. Together, these studies demonstrate the effectiveness and growing adoption of LLM-based MAS for software engineering tasks. However, improving their real-world deployment requires a deeper understanding of the challenges practitioners encounter, their underlying causes, and potential solutions.

6.3 Exploration of Issues, Causes, and Solutions in LLM-based MAS

While existing studies have demonstrated the potential of LLM-based MAS for software engineering tasks, recent research has started investigating the practical challenges, limitations, and failure patterns of these systems. Liu et al. (2025) conducted an empirical study of open-source LLM-based MAS frameworks by analyzing over 42,000 commits and 4,700 resolved issues across eight frameworks. They identified common development and maintenance issues, including bugs, infrastructure problems, and agent coordination challenges, highlighting the difficulties in building reliable MAS. Similarly, (Asgari et al., 2026) investigated developer challenges in LLM-based MAS frameworks through Stack Overflow discussions and GitHub issues. Their study identified several challenges related to retrieval, agent memory, orchestration, execution control, and runtime reliability, which affect the development and maintenance of LLM-based MAS frameworks. Furthermore, Hamid et al. (2026) explored practitioner difficulties in agentic frameworks by analyzing 2,658 Stack Overflow posts. They identified challenges related to framework configuration, tool integration, vector database operations, and agent execution behavior, with runtime-related issues emerging as particularly challenging to address. In addition, Cemri et al. (2025) analyzed over 1,600 execution traces from seven LLM-based MAS frameworks and proposed the MAS Failure Taxonomy (MAST), identifying 14 failure modes across different stages of agent execution. These studies provide insights into LLM-based MAS challenges and failure patterns; however, a comprehensive understanding of practitioner-reported issues, their causes, and solutions remains limited. This study addresses this gap through empirical analysis of the issues of LLM-based MAS.

6.4 Conclusive Summary

Software repository mining has been widely used to investigate practitioner-reported issues, their root causes, and solutions in software systems, providing a foundation for understanding real-world development challenges (Waseem et al., 2026). With the increasing adoption of LLMs in software engineering, researchers have extended repository mining approaches to study issues in LLM-based software systems (Cai et al., 2025b). Recently, LLM-based MAS have attracted significant attention by enabling multiple LLM-powered specialized agents to collaboratively perform complex software engineering tasks beyond the capabilities of single-agent LLMs, leading to the development of various frameworks and techniques, such as ChatDev and AgileCoder (Qian et al., 2024; Nguyen et al., 2025). However, relatively few studies have investigated the practical issues, failure patterns, and maintenance challenges of LLM-based MAS (Liu et al., 2025; Cemri et al., 2025). Consequently, existing studies on LLM-based MAS provide only limited understanding of the practical problems faced by practitioners, their underlying causes, and the solutions adopted in real-world LLM-based MAS projects. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical analysis of closed GitHub issues from LLM-based MAS projects to derive taxonomies of issues, their underlying causes, and solutions. The comparison with existing studies is summarized in Table 10.

7 Conclusions

In this study, we investigated the issues that practitioners encounter when developing and using open-source LLM-based MAS, as well as their underlying causes and potential solutions. We collected 22,848 closed issues from open-source LLM-based MAS on GitHub that met our inclusion criteria, as shown in Table 2. Then, we applied a mixed automated and manual filtering approach to reduce the dataset to 944 issues related to LLM-based MAS. Finally, we extracted 944 issues, 540 causes, and 427 solutions based on our data extraction criteria. Our results show that Orchestration & Execution Issue is the most common issue faced by practitioners. Workflow Problem (WP), Tool Integration Problem (TIP), and Memory Problem (MP) are identified as the most frequent causes of the issues, while Optimize Workflow (OW) was employed as the predominant solution to address the issues.

Based on the study results, we provide implications for users, developers, and researchers of open-source LLM-based MAS. Users can address the most frequent Orchestration & Execution Issue through explicit handoff design between agents and multi-agent execution controls, such as retry limits, timeouts, and monitoring mechanisms in LLM-based MAS. They can also refine prompt design to obtain more reliable responses from LLM-based MAS. Developers can improve tool integration reliability through schema validation, execution controls, and tool connection management in LLM-based MAS. Researchers can explore methods to reproduce and diagnose unsolved issues and develop reliable memory management mechanisms to improve context propagation between agents, state synchronization across agents, and memory retrieval for agent interactions in LLM-based MAS.

The dataset used in this study is available in the replication package (Rehman et al., 2026).

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.

We gratefully acknowledge support from our major funders, member institutions, , and all contributors.
